POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 22 Oct 2026 08:32:41 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Adipositas: Sparen kann für den Staat teuer werden https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-content/adipositas-sparen-kann-fuer-den-staat-teuer-werden/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 08:17:53 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=sponsored-content&p=9144305 Nach Berechnungen des Gesundheitsökonomen Dr. Tobias Effertz und seiner Kollegen verursacht Adipositas in Deutschland jährlich rund 63 Milliarden Euro an Kosten. Knapp 29 Milliarden Euro entfallen auf direkte medizinische Ausgaben, etwa für Arztbesuche, Behandlungen und Rehabilitation. Rund 34 Milliarden Euro entstehen indirekt durch krankheitsbedingte Fehlzeiten, eingeschränkte Leistungsfähigkeit oder vorzeitige Verrentung. Mit diesen Zahlen stehen die Wissenschaftler nicht allein, auch das WifOR Institut kommt zu einer vergleichbaren Größenordnung. Die Nationale Akademie der Wissenschaften Leopoldina veranschlagt die Belastung für Übergewicht und Adipositas unter Einbeziehung weiterer Kosten sogar deutlich höher. Die Studien unterscheiden sich je nach Methodik. Doch eines zeigen sie übereinstimmend: Die wirtschaftliche Dimension der Erkrankung geht weit über die Ausgaben einzelner Krankenkassen hinaus.

Adipositas ist keine reine Lifestyle-Frage. Die chronische Erkrankung entsteht durch ein komplexes Zusammenspiel biologischer, genetischer, sozialer und umweltbezogener Faktoren. Nach Angaben des Robert Koch-Instituts lebt inzwischen etwa jeder fünfte Erwachsene in Deutschland mit Adipositas. Zu Beginn der 2000er-Jahre lag der Anteil mit etwa 12 Prozent noch deutlich niedriger. Die Leopoldina spricht deshalb bereits von einer „Adipositas-Epidemie“.

Der englische Weg der Adipositas-Versorgung

Das deutsche Gesundheitssystem beschränkt sich auf die Behandlung von Folgeerkrankungen der Adipositas, etwa Typ-2-Diabetes oder Herz-Kreislauf-Erkrankungen. Deren Behandlung ist medizinisch notwendig. Die politische Frage lautet jedoch, ob es auf Dauer wirtschaftlich sinnvoll ist, vor allem die Folgen der Adipositas zu finanzieren, anstatt Adipositas direkt zu behandeln. Das ist vor dem Hintergrund des demografischen Wandels und mangelnder Fachkräfte besonders relevant. Eine vom Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft veröffentlichte Prognose geht davon aus, dass Deutschland bis 2036 rund 4,3 Millionen Arbeitskräfte fehlen könnten. Adipositas ist nicht die Ursache des Fachkräftemangels und auch nicht die alleinige Lösung. Sie ist aber ein Faktor, der die Erwerbsfähigkeit beeinträchtigen kann. Eine Gesundheitspolitik, die Menschen länger gesund im Arbeitsleben halten will, muss solche Zusammenhänge berücksichtigen.

Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht.

Der Blick ins Ausland zeigt, dass die politische Debatte über die Versorgung von Adipositas auch anders geführt werden kann. In England hat der staatliche Gesundheitsdienst NHS mit einem stufenweisen Rollout medikamentöser Therapien begonnen. Vorgesehen ist der Zugang zunächst für Erwachsene mit einem Body-Mass-Index von mindestens 35 kg/m2 und mindestens einer Begleiterkrankung. Die Behandlung erfolgt über spezialisierte Dienste und soll zunehmend auch in Hausarztpraxen angeboten werden. Grundlage sind Empfehlungen des englischen Instituts NICE. Nach dessen Schätzungen könnten in England rund 3,4 Millionen Erwachsene grundsätzlich die Kriterien für eine Behandlung erfüllen.

Das englische Modell setzt auf definierte medizinische Kriterien, einen schrittweisen Zugang und die Einbettung in bestehende Versorgungsstrukturen. Gerade darin liegt der gesundheitspolitische Unterschied zu der Debatte in Deutschland. Hierzulande richtet sich der Blick fast reflexartig auf die Kosten moderner Arzneimittel und Therapien. Das ist angesichts knapper Kassen nachvollziehbar, greift aber zu kurz. Entscheidend ist nicht allein, ob eine Therapie kurzfristig zusätzliche Kosten verursacht. Zu berücksichtigen sind ebenso Kosten unbehandelter oder zu spät behandelter Erkrankungen und demgegenüber mögliche Einsparungen durch vermiedene Folgeerkrankungen, weniger Arbeitsausfälle und einen längeren Verbleib im Erwerbsleben. Für Deutschland stellt sich also die grundsätzliche Frage: Soll die medikamentöse Behandlung von Adipositas weiterhin aus der Regelversorgung ausgeschlossen bleiben oder braucht es, ähnlich wie in England, einen zielgerichteten und stufenweisen Zugang für Menschen mit Adipositas?

Gesundheit als Investition

Eine moderne Adipositas-Versorgung ist eine Investition in die Stabilität von Gesundheitswesen, Arbeitsmarkt und Sozialversicherung zugleich. Zugelassene medikamentöse Therapien sollten dort eingesetzt werden können, wo sie medizinisch angezeigt sind. Ernährungs-, Bewegungs- und Verhaltenstherapie bleiben auch weiterhin wichtige Bestandteile, reichen aber in manchen Fällen nicht aus. Notwendig ist ein Versorgungskonzept, das Prävention, Früherkennung und leitliniengerechte Behandlung verbindet.

Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.

Gerade in Zeiten knapper Kassen verlangt ein verantwortungsvoller Haushalt eine vollständige Kostenrechnung. Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht allein, was eine Behandlung kostet, sondern auch, welche Kosten durch Nichtbehandlung entstehen. Wer nur kurzfristige Ausgaben betrachtet, riskiert, langfristig höhere Belastungen zu finanzieren.

The Vienna-based agency warned that there are serious risks to fundamental rights at the bloc’s external borders and the sudden arrival of thousands of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July “put the balance between protecting fundamental rights and safeguarding the EU’s external borders to the test.”  

In late July, more than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in the space of 48 hours, leading to questions about how the EU should deal with sudden mass movements that may be engineered or used against the bloc. In her State of the Union address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised a European emergency response framework, which she said should allow for “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.”

Greece has called for a measure suspending asylum applications in emergency situations — something that could amount to pushbacks, which are banned under international law. Several countries have thrown their support behind the idea, while others question whether this type of measure should be taken at the level of the EU, rather than in national capitals.

In its report, the agency said any emergency measure should comply with EU and international law, both of which guarantee the right to seek asylum and the principle of non-refoulement — a “cornerstone of refugee protection,” it added.

At a meeting of EU leaders last week, von der Leyen said the Commission would come up with a proposal for the emergency framework before the end of the year. 

“We will always uphold our values and fundamental rights, but we will never compromise on protecting our borders,” she said.

The agency’s report also highlighted other fundamental rights concerns at the EU’s external borders, including the implementation of rights monitoring mechanisms as part of migration reforms, restrictions on search and rescue organizations, and investigations into rights violations at the borders.

According to the agency’s numbers, 12 EU countries opened 322 preliminary criminal investigations between 2020 and 2025, but only nine of those resulted in a conviction.

Gaps in those investigations “lead to a perception of impunity, which risks undermining the rule of law, one of the fundamental values on which the Union is founded,” the report stated.

]]> de Cyberangriffe kommen nicht nur zu Bürozeiten https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-content/cyberangriffe-kommen-nicht-nur-zu-buerozeiten/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=sponsored-content&p=9170288 An diesem Vormittag wartet die IT-Abteilung von Babor auf einen Cyberangriff. Genauer gesagt auf das Ergebnis eines Cyberangriffs, den sie selbst in Auftrag gegeben hat: Ein Penetrationstest soll zeigen, wie gut die Systeme des Kosmetikherstellers geschützt sind. Denn die Bedrohungslage verändert sich. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie Unternehmen arbeiten, sondern auch, wie sie angegriffen werden. Phishing-Mails lassen sich heute in Sekunden auf ihre Opfer zuschneiden, Schadsoftware kann sich automatisiert an Abwehrmechanismen anpassen, und Angriffsmuster entwickeln sich schneller weiter, als klassische Sicherheitskonzepte nachziehen können. Für Unternehmen werden damit zwei Fragen immer wichtiger: Wie schnell erkennen sie einen Angriff und wie reagieren sie darauf?

Ein Härtetest für die IT-Sicherheit

Gemeinsam mit den Expertinnen und Experten von Vodafone und SITS hat das Team die eigene IT-Infrastruktur einem kontrollierten Cyberangriff ausgesetzt. Die Frage ist, wie gut die Systeme einem echten Angreifer standhalten würden und vor allem, wie früh ein solcher Angriff erkannt wird. „Das Ergebnis haben wir mit Spannung erwartet“, sagt Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor. Für die IT-Abteilung ist der Test mehr als eine technische Übung. Babor betreibt rund 200 Server am Hauptsitz in Aachen, dazu kommen weitere Rechenzentrumsstrukturen an unterschiedlichen Standorten. ERP-Systeme, Datenbanken und Kollaborationstools bilden die Grundlage der täglichen Geschäftsprozesse. Weltweit vernetzte Standorte mit Tochtergesellschaften in Europa und Nordamerika sowie mehr als 1000 Mitarbeitern machen die Infrastruktur zusätzlich komplex. Entsprechend hoch sind die Anforderungen an ihre Absicherung. Die bisher eingesetzte Sicherheitslösung stieß zunehmend an ihre Grenzen. Gesucht war ein Ansatz, der nicht nur automatisiert auf verdächtige Aktivitäten reagiert, sondern die gesamte Infrastruktur rund um die Uhr im Blick behält und bei Bedarf Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten hinzuzieht. Inzwischen ist ein solches Security Operations Center (SOC) bei Babor im Einsatz. Der Penetrationstest sollte deshalb auch zeigen, wie gut die neue Sicherheitsarchitektur im Ernstfall funktioniert.

Der Moment der Wahrheit

Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.

Endlich liegen die Ergebnisse des Tests auf dem Tisch. Die Anspannung weicht der Erleichterung. „Wir waren dann aber ein Stück weit beruhigt: Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.“ Der Test zeigt damit zweierlei: Die vorhandenen Schutzmechanismen greifen und das Zusammenspiel aus automatisierter Erkennung und der Analyse durch Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten funktioniert. Gleichzeitig wird deutlich, dass IT-Sicherheit eine Aufgabe ist, die kontinuierliche Aufmerksamkeit erfordert. Denn ein Angriff hält sich nicht an Bürozeiten, und eine IT-Abteilung kann nicht rund um die Uhr vor den Bildschirmen sitzen.

Die Lösung: Security Operations Center

Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Das externe Security Operations Center übernimmt für Babor die kontinuierliche Überwachung der IT-Infrastruktur und kombiniert automatisierte Prozesse mit der Analyse durch erfahrene Security Expertinnen oder -Experten. Sicherheitsrelevante Ereignisse werden fortlaufend analysiert, Auffälligkeiten bewertet und bei Bedarf entsprechende Maßnahmen eingeleitet. Für die interne IT bedeutet das eine zusätzliche Sicherheitsebene und zugleich mehr Freiraum für andere Aufgaben. Statt sämtliche sicherheitsrelevanten Ereignisse selbst rund um die Uhr überwachen und einordnen zu müssen, kann das Babor-Team auf die Expertise der SOC-Spezialisten zurückgreifen. Auch Anforderungen, die über den reinen Schutz der IT-Systeme hinausgehen, lassen sich auf diese Weise berücksichtigen. Dazu zählen etwa Vorgaben aus dem Bereich Compliance oder Anforderungen der Cyberversicherung. Das SOC schafft damit eine Struktur, in der Sicherheitsereignisse kontinuierlich beobachtet und nach definierten Prozessen bearbeitet werden können. Für Rüdiger Mohnen, IT Leiter von Babor, macht sich die Unterstützung bereits im Arbeitsalltag bemerkbar: „Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns voll auf unser Kerngeschäft konzentrieren können. Wir wissen, dass unser Firmennetz durch eine zusätzliche Instanz zuverlässig geschützt ist und haben im Ernstfall jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite. Für mittelständische Unternehmen ist der Verzicht auf ein SOC aus meiner Sicht fahrlässig.“ Der Cyberangriff an diesem Vormittag war kontrolliert. Die nächste Attacke wird es möglicherweise nicht sein. Für Babor kommt es deshalb darauf an, Bedrohungen nicht erst dann zu erkennen, wenn sie Schaden angerichtet haben. Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Eine zusätzliche Schutzinstanz

Drei Fragen an Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor, und Rüdiger Mohnen, IT-Leiter von Babor.

Warum setzt Babor beim Schutz seines Firmennetzes auf ein externes Security Operations Center?

Mirella Fiebes: Für uns war entscheidend, ein durchgängiges 24/7-Monitoring sicherzustellen. Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Rüdiger Mohnen: Zuverlässiger Cyberschutz ist für uns essenziell – nicht zuletzt im Hinblick auf Compliance-Anforderungen und die Vorgaben unserer Cyberversicherung. Ausfälle infolge von Cyberangriffen würden schnell erhebliche Kosten verursachen.

Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Welche konkreten Vorteile bringt Ihnen das SOC?

Rüdiger Mohnen: Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns konsequent auf unser Kerngeschäft fokussieren können. Gleichzeitig gewinnen wir zusätzliche Sicherheit durch eine unabhängige Instanz sowie durch die enge Zusammenarbeit mit den Security-Expert:innen. Im Ernstfall haben wir jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite.

Warum haben Sie sich für Vodafone Business als Partner entschieden?

Mirella Fiebes: Das Angebot von Vodafone hat uns inhaltlich und konzeptionell überzeugt. Diese Entscheidung wurde sowohl in der Implementierungsphase – gemeinsam mit dem Partner SITS – als auch im laufenden Betrieb bestätigt.

]]> de Trump’s diesel deal derailed Ukraine-Russia peace progress, says Czech president https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-trump-diesel-deal-derailed-ukraine-russia-peace-progress-says-czech-president-petr-pavel/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 02:02:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9202589 Czech President Petr Pavel says a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine was “quite close” – until President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. 

In an interview conducted on Tuesday with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which includes POLITICO, Pavel said coordinated U.S.-European sanctions on Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries were putting Russia “under strain.” But the deal Trump announced earlier this month, in which Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S., gave Russia “time to breathe.”

“It will be much harder now,” said Pavel. “Russia uses this momentum to get out of pressure, and it’s kind of a moral boost for them.”

The White House on Wednesday said Trump “successfully negotiated” the deal in order to supply the global market with “massive amounts of diesel and bring prices down.”

The deal quickly drew backlash and, at one point, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators urged Trump to rescind the deal.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media that the deal “plays into Russia’s hands” and allows Russia “to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world.” He accused Trump of using peace talks in Florida as a “smokescreen” as the administration pursued its deal with Russia.

Zelenskyy’s criticism was the latest indicator of rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Trump has repeatedly expressed frustrations with Zelenskyy, accusing him of elongating the war. By contrast, of late he has spoken warmly of Putin and said this week that “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine.” 

But Pavel offered the Ukrainian president words of support on Wednesday. 

“I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict,” said Pavel. “So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia.”

He added that Trump shows a more open approach to Russia than any European leader. 

“To some extent, he may be attracted by Vladimir Putin as a leader with authority, but I don’t think that … President Trump sees it from a position of a struggle between democracy and autocracies because he’s looking at it simply from the point of view of economic prosperity for the United States,” Pavel added.  

Though Pavel indicated concerns about the diesel deal, he declined to say the U.S. had betrayed Ukraine or other European partners. 

“I don’t know yet if we can call it betrayal, but I would call it a mistake,” he said. “Because … it’s now giving Russia a new hope: New hope that they can disregard Europe, they can disregard Ukraine, they can focus on making a deal with the United States, potentially with China, and arranging all things up to their priorities and strategies. I believe that it’s clearly against our interest in Europe.”

Pavel also didn’t rule out a future in which European countries would buy Russian oil, but added that it “will take time” before that happens. 

“If one day Russia is a country respecting other countries’ sovereignty and borders, why not have regular business with such a country? But Russia is not there yet,” he said.

]]> en Far-right Italian general hunts the manosphere vote https://www.politico.eu/article/roberto-vannacci-far-right-italy-manosphere-vote/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9161372 ROME — Former paratrooper General Roberto Vannacci portrays himself on social media as a Roman legionary and charioteer. He has declared he prefers women “without skirts” and posted an AI-generated image of a female junior minister with exaggerated cleavage.

None of these projections of masculinity and anti-woke culture are clumsy gaffes. The insurgent far-right star of Italian politics is making a deliberate play to the so-called manosphere to transform himself from an internet provocateur into a heavyweight political force.

For Italy’s first female prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, Vannacci now poses a serious problem as she needs to decide whether he is an asset or a liability. With elections expected next spring, his National Future party is polling at about 8%, making him a potentially crucial factor in building a right-wing coalition.

“It is disgusting to think you can manipulate the image of a woman for such deplorable propaganda,” the center-right junior minister in Meloni’s coalition whose image was manipulated, Matilde Siracusano, told POLITICO.  “I don’t think we have ever sunk this low, especially from someone aspiring to be a national political leader.”

Vannacci’s provocations may look like familiar trolling from a politician who has built his reputation on saying the unsayable. But behind them lies a broader political project, tapping into the grievances of young men who feel alienated by feminism and progressive culture.

Emanuele Pozzolo, a National Future parliamentarian who defected from Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, believes young men have become increasingly constrained in their relationships with women.

“I think young Western men are very often almost castrated in their instinct for dealing with women,” he said, arguing that even legitimate romantic approaches risk being treated as aggression. 

“The cultural problem is that sometimes everything seems to be harassment, everything abuse, everything violence,” he added, while stressing that genuine abuse must be punished.

Mediterranean patriarchy

Vannacci combines inflammatory online messaging and an alpha-male persona with a political program that promises to restore traditional roles for men and women. National Future even has a name for its preferred social order: “Mediterranean patriarchy.”

Its political program calls for the formation of “strong men” capable of controlling their emotions and passions, protecting women and sacrificing themselves for society. It opposes the recently introduced crime of femicide, condemns feminism, and declares the defense of life “from conception to natural death” and the “natural family” among its non-negotiable values.

The architect of this vision and principal author of the program is Lorenzo Gasperini, a conservative Catholic philosophy teacher from Tuscany, who has opposed vaccines and abortion rights on social media and blamed feminism for violence against women.

The result is a political offering that combines different traditions: conservative Catholic ideas about family and sexuality, older Italian ideas of virility and the much newer online politics of male grievance.

The manifesto seeks to put traditional family values into practice with proposals to pay parents who leave work to raise children, and reward parents of large families with tax exemption and public sector jobs.  

Some proposals echo Benito Mussolini’s fascist-era “Battle for Births,” which offered similar incentives while promoting motherhood as a patriotic duty.

Luca Sforzini, a former Vannacci ideologue who has since broken with him, said the Mediterranean label was a clever piece of marketing.

“It’s like talking about the Mediterranean diet,” he told POLITICO. “You think of Italian food, mozzarella, tomatoes, olive oil.” The result, he said, was to conceal a patriarchal model with men above women behind “bucolic, positive images. It’s monstrous,” he said.

Pozzolo rejected the suggestion that the program advocates for male supremacy.

“It is exactly the opposite,” he said. “When we talk about Mediterranean patriarchy, the main idea is to recover, preserve and pass on the responsibilities of being a man within the family and society.” Men, he argued, had a duty to show women respect, love and protection, while rejecting violence or coercive control.

He defended the “without skirts” remark as “extremely funny” — picking up on a reference to Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani advocating long skirts — and not remotely offensive, comparing Vannacci’s ability to connect with ordinary Italians to Silvio Berlusconi’s. 

At a recent rally in the Umbrian city of Orvieto, Vannacci defended the Mediterranean patriarchy concept as not “oppression and possession” but “duty, fidelity, sacrifice,” and said it was the family model that had allowed “us to prevail over the last 2,000 years.”

Elisa Ercoli, president of the women’s rights organization Differenza Donna, condemned the program as “a return to the supremacy of the white, cisgender alpha male, and the woman as his handmaiden.”

Appealing to alphas

Vannacci, who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, became a media sensation in 2023 with the self-published book “The World Upside Down,” a broadside against immigration, feminism and homosexuality. In it, he told gay people: “You are not normal, get over it.”

Lionized by fans as a defender of common sense against progressive politics, he received more than half a million votes as a candidate for the anti-immigration League in the 2024 European elections, before founding National Future in February.

Polling analysis suggests that about 62% of National Future’s prospective voters are male, including strong support among manual workers and the unemployed.

Pozzolo denied National Future was deliberately targeting male voters, insisting the party’s ambition was to reach Italians of all backgrounds who felt unrepresented.

Federica Formato, a lecturer at Brighton University in the U.K., who studies gender and the far right, said Vannacci was “testing the waters” to see whether he can reach a younger male audience, tapping into what she described as the “aggrieved entitlement” of young men.

A career soldier, he has repeatedly portrayed himself through images of physical strength, competition and military prowess. On social media, AI-generated versions proliferate of Vannacci as an ancient Roman in scenes recalling the Ridley Scott epic Gladiator.

For Formato, the Roman imagery projects “virility and hyper-masculinity,” while Vannacci’s army background itself helps construct the image of an “alpha male.”

Humor, memes and deliberate provocation are particularly effective with a younger online audience, Formato said, allowing relatively complex ideological messages to be reduced to instantly comprehensible images. “He is not naive,” she said. “He says things to provoke and get more attention.”

That presents Meloni with a headache. Vannacci’s party is drawing voters from her Brothers of Italy and Matteo Salvini’s League, while offering a more uncompromising platform on immigration, social issues and foreign policy.

Yet Vannacci has opened the door to an alliance with Meloni if she needs his votes. He has described National Future as a natural partner for the center-right, while insisting that any deal must respect his party’s principles. With Italy’s new electoral law offering a parliamentary majority bonus to coalitions winning at least 42 percent of the vote, those votes could matter.

That presents Meloni with an uncomfortable choice: Keep Vannacci outside the coalition, or bring into her government a movement whose appeal rests partly on the grievances of men who believe feminism has gone too far.

For Formato, Vannacci is exploiting a space in Italian politics that has so far lacked a figure capable of turning those grievances into an organized political constituency.

Vannacci, with his promises to restore traditional masculinity, appears determined to occupy it.

“There is an empty chair,” she said.

]]> en Ukraine’s foreign fighters battle Russians — and red tape https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-foreign-fighters-face-bureaucratic-hurdles-residency-permits/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9175469 KYIV — Jordan O’Brien has fought for Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, including during the 2022 liberation of Kherson and the 2024 incursion into Russia’s Kursk region. But after years of service, O’Brien says he would warn other foreigners against joining up, citing the bureaucratic problems he has faced.

O’Brien, a New Zealander, complained about red tape and a state apparatus that appears to have little understanding and compassion for people volunteering to fight for a foreign country. If that isn’t fixed, Ukraine may have a harder time attracting desperately needed recruits, hampering its effort to continue resisting Russia.

“If Kyiv wants more foreign fighters, it needs to fix the ridiculous bureaucratic bias that screws all of us foreigners over who have already fought for Ukraine,” said O’Brien, who has been sentenced in absentia by Russia to 14 years in prison for fighting alongside Ukraine.

As of August, the defense ministry said some 16,000 foreigners from 72 countries were serving in the Ukrainian armed forces, giving crucial help to a 900,000-strong military that is chronically short of recruits.

The volunteers are facing a looming deadline. The Ukrainian parliament last year passed a law mandating that foreigners serving in the military have to file paperwork by Nov. 10 to get temporary residence permits.

“If nothing changes, then after November 10, a significant number of the foreigners defending Ukraine will technically be in the country illegally,” Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan said in a social media post.

That clashes with the official recruitment information given to foreign volunteers, which says their contract “is the basis for legal long-term stay in Ukraine.”

“Even though I can prove I was serving in the Ukrainian army, they still make it impossible for us foreigners; none of them have any respect for people who fight for Ukraine, and they treat us like illegal aliens,” O’Brien said.

“I have been in three different Ukrainian units, and all of them have made mistakes in my military contracts or done them in a way that is not legally correct, so when I go to immigration to apply for the residency that I fought hard for, they ended up giving me a fine that I had to pay on the spot because my information was incorrect in my contract,” O’Brien added.

The Ukrainian military ombudsman’s office has fielded more than 300 complaints this year from foreign volunteers and their families related to granting combatant status, early termination of contracts at the soldier’s request and ensuring timely medical care.

In a report for the Washington-based Center for European Policy Analysis think tank, an American volunteer said that neither he nor most of his comrades had received their UBD — the document confirming combat participation that opens the door to veteran status in Ukraine.

Part of the issue is due to an uneven transition from paper identification to digital military IDs that has left out many foreign volunteers.

A study by the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper earlier this year found that language barriers are a big problem, especially for Spanish-speaking Colombians who constitute the largest group of foreign service members. The study also found that if a veteran has been discharged from the Ukrainian forces, they can sometimes face deportation.

Kyiv is waking up to the problem.

 “We highly value everyone’s contribution and fully recognize the state’s responsibility to uphold their rights and legitimate interests,” said Liudmyla Kalenchuk, head of the soldiers’ rights department in Ukraine’s military ombudsman’s office.

Last month, the defense ministry started a working group aimed at improving terms of service, legalization and treatment of foreign soldiers and their families. The Ukrainian parliament is also working on legislation to simplify and extend deadlines to legalize the stay of foreign fighters in the country and lift other bureaucratic burdens.

“Many foreign fighters are unable to complete the process of obtaining a residence permit, as they are carrying out combat missions far from their unit’s base and cannot simultaneously gather the necessary documents and visit the migration service,” said Halan. 

Kalenchuk argued that legalization problems are not widespread, but did say there are vulnerable categories of service members — for instance, those who lost their passports while serving, including citizens of Russia, Belarus and South Africa.

Foreign fighters

Ukraine opened its doors to foreign volunteers like O’Brien in the first hours of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, when the country’s survival was at stake, said Meaghan Mobbs, president of the R.T. Weatherman Foundation, an NGO helping war veterans and their families.

“No one could have predicted either the extraordinary number of foreigners who would answer that call or that Russia’s war of aggression would continue at this scale for years,” Mobbs said. “What began as an emergency wartime mechanism became something much larger and more permanent. The system now has to catch up.”

Russia also recruits foreign fighters, many from poorer countries keen to get cash or Russian citizenship. Its North Korean allies are also fighting alongside Russian forces.

Ukraine offers foreigners a freedom-fighting cause, combat experience, deals worth up to $10,000 per month for dangerous front-line duty and the possibility of quitting the three-year contract after six months of service. The pay is the same as that received by Ukrainian soldiers.

About 8,000 foreign volunteers serve in the ground forces, while the remaining 8,000 are dispersed among the National Guard, special transport service and other units, said Kalenchuk.

In its recruitment information, Ukraine says volunteers should be between 18 and 60 years of age, fit, legally allowed to enter Ukraine, andthat military and combat experience is an advantage. Only people who understand English, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian or Ukrainian are accepted.

The flow of foreign recruits is growing, from some 100 a month in 2022 to 600 a month now. About 40% come from Latin America.

Most come to Ukraine to help fight against Russia, while some add that pay and the opportunity to gain combat experience are also motivating factors, Kalenchuk said.

Ukrainian units have differing abilities to receive, train, communicate with and administer foreign personnel.

“Foreign volunteers themselves also vary enormously in experience, capability and motivation. Ukraine has learned a tremendous amount since 2022 about what makes a foreign volunteer genuinely valuable, and those lessons should shape what comes next,” Mobbs said.

Family complaints

As well as red tape linked to residence status, foreign fighters also complain about not being paid, not being given adequate medical care, the lack of official combatant status that gives social benefits and protections, and inadequate provision of food and military supplies, the military ombudsman’s office said.

There is also criticism over how Ukrainian bureaucracy deals with the families of volunteers.

More than 10% of the complaints to the ombudsman’s office come from families requesting official confirmation of whether a volunteer is missing or has been killed in action, Kalenchuk said.

“For me, this is where the shortcomings become very personal. These are mothers, fathers, wives and children whose loved ones traveled thousands of miles to defend a country that was not their own. Some families have told us they feel forgotten after that sacrifice — or even maligned when they ask difficult questions or push for answers. That should never happen,” Mobbs said.

According to her, some families have learned of deaths from fellow soldiers, or via social media, before receiving official notification. Families can spend months navigating military units, ministries, diplomatic missions, identification and repatriation procedures, and compensation and benefits under Ukrainian law without one clear pathway or person responsible for guiding them.

Wounded volunteers are entitled to free medical treatment and a special payout in the event of disability. Families of fallen soldiers receive compensation of 15 million hryvnia (€300,000).

“Grief is difficult enough without having to become an expert in the bureaucracy of a foreign country at war,” Mobbs added.

However, she said there is reason for optimism. The Weatherman Foundation helped organize a meeting between Halan, the deputy defense minister, and families of nine American volunteers who were killed or went missing.

“What mattered to me was that she listened. The families were able to explain directly what had happened to them and where the system had failed them. The ministry is now working on administrative and legislative changes, and we are committed to helping turn those experiences into solutions,” Mobbs said.

The ministry will take this experience into account in its work on supporting foreign military personnel and their families, Halan said.

“They are sons of their own homeland, yet in a moment of crisis, they became brothers to the Ukrainian people and soldiers in the Ukrainian army. Therefore, we have an obligation to ensure that their families receive high-quality support at every stage of their interaction with the Ukrainian state,” Halan added.  

Unless the country’s approach to foreign volunteers changes, O’Brien said he would warn potential volunteers against signing up.

“The military HR system and the civilian departments need significant change because right now I tell everyone to stay away from Ukraine, because you won’t be looked after if anything goes wrong and even with a lawyer on my side it’s an uphill battle to do anything,” O’Brien said.

But when asked if he regrets fighting alongside Ukrainians against Russia since 2022, O’Brien said no.

“I joined because Russia is a terrorist regime that needs to be stopped,” he said, adding: “I stay with Ukraine because it is the people that I fight for, not [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy or the government or the departments who continue to fuck us over again and again, but the everyday Ukrainians who just want to live in peace.”

]]> en Merz’s eastern nightmare is far from over https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-friedrich-merz-cdu-eastern-nightmare-is-far-from-over/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 22 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9200816 BERLIN — Friedrich Merz has tried to move on from his conservatives’ historic defeats to the far right in eastern Germany, but his biggest test as chancellor — and of his grip over his own party — may still lie ahead.

The Alternative for Germany is pushing to deliver its biggest blow yet to the chancellor’s weakened coalition government by installing the country’s first far-right state premier since World War II in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt when lawmakers vote on the post in December.

Merz’s fellow Christian Democrats in Berlin fear regional members of their own party will help the AfD do this, creating a nightmare scenario for the chancellor. That concern stems from accusations that a group of Saxony-Anhalt conservatives already broke ranks by voting in a secret ballot for the AfD’s candidate for state speaker earlier this month, outraging national conservative leaders.

“The behavior of the CDU parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt with regard to past and upcoming elections is completely unacceptable,” Thomas Röwekamp, a CDU lawmaker who chairs the Bundestag’s defense committee, said. The AfD “wants to annihilate the CDU in Germany” by “forcing us into a debate about how to deal with it in order to divide the party,” he added. “We must not allow that to happen.”

Under pressure from conservatives in Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt CDU leader Sven Schulze announced a plan last week to have his party’s lawmakers leave the chamber during the initial two rounds of secret voting in December, ensuring none can vote for the far-right candidate — or be suspected of doing so. It’s unclear what the party would do in a potential third round, when the AfD would only need a majority of votes cast.

AfD leaders have openly said they are seeking defections from conservative ranks, a strategy designed as much to sow division among conservatives as to win the premiership. That approach seems to be working, at least partly.

State conservatives have faced intense criticism for appearing so divided and vulnerable to aiding the AfD that their leaders apparently have no choice but to avoid the vote altogether. “It’s about taking a stand and assuming responsibility, rather than shirking a decision,” Röwekamp said.

Local CDU lawmakers, however, say their approach is tactically necessary.  “We have always drawn a clear line between ourselves and the AfD,” CDU state lawmaker Chris Schulenburg said. “We adhere to the principle of distinguishing ourselves on the basis of substance, but not excluding them [the AfD], because, after all, the party is not currently banned, and its parliamentarians were also democratically elected.”

AfD leaders, meanwhile, have rejoiced in the CDU’s disarray.

“This is nothing less than the CDU’s capitulation,” AfD national co-leader Tino Chrupalla said after the state conservatives announced their plan to leave the chamber. “They’re afraid of elections.”

Centrists flirting with radicals

For Merz, whose approval ratings are at historic lows, his party’s conduct in Saxony-Anhalt — and the prospect of a politically explosive AfD victory in December — are complicating efforts to move past last month’s humiliating election losses in eastern Germany and project renewed control as he attempts to focus on core priorities: backing Ukraine and reviving the economy.

Already, center-left lawmakers have attacked parts of Merz’s party as having failed to learn the lessons of Germany’s history, drawing parallels with the Nazis’ rise to power with conservative help.

After local conservative lawmakers appeared to back the AfD’s candidate for the Saxony-Anhalt speaker earlier this month, Social Democratic Party (SPD) lawmakers in Berlin marched in protest past the Brandenburg Gate to a square where the Nazis carried out book burnings. SPD Defense Minister Boris Pistorius sang the national anthem and called the episode the breaking of a taboo that “we haven’t seen in this form for more than 90 years.”

Conservative lawmakers have retorted in recent weeks by attacking the SPD and Greens for letting their Berlin branches enter coalition talks with the Left — a far-left party rooted in the East German communist party— which won first in the city in last month’s election.

But for Merz and his coalition government, the stakes of the December vote in Saxony-Anhalt are far greater.

How the December vote will unfold remains highly unpredictable. Ultimately, the AfD’s candidate for the premiership, Ulrich Siegmund, could win the post with support from Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, a small, populist-left party that has expressed openness to working with the AfD and shares its Kremlin-friendly views.

Merz is clearly alarmed by the prospect of CDU lawmakers covertly assisting the AfD — an outcome that could trigger his chancellorship’s greatest political crisis yet.

“People who do things like that — members of parliament who extend a hand — there is no place in the CDU for such a choice, and that will not change,” Merz said earlier this month. “The CDU will never elect extremists to public office or government positions anywhere in Germany.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 22 Oct 2026 08:42:17 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Polish parliament liberalises abortion law – but conservative president likely to veto changes https://euobserver.com/244109/polish-parliament-liberalises-abortion-law-but-conservative-president-likely-to-veto-changes/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 08:42:17 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244109 The Polish governing coalition voted in parliament to loosen abortion law on Tuesday - but conservative president is expected to block the change. ]]> Poland’s governing coalition voted in parliament to loosen abortion law on Tuesday (20 October) – but the country’s conservative president is expected to block the change.

Poland has one of Europe’s harshest abortion laws, allowing only two exceptions to a general ban: in case of rape or danger to the woman’s health.

The amendments, passed by a narrow majority, would allow for abortions in cases of severe deformation of the foetus, and partially decriminalise helping others terminate their pregnancy.

Currently, doctors fear facing up to three years in prison for performing an illegal abortion. At least six women have died because they were denied an abortion in the last six years.

]]> EU prosecutors raid far-right Patriots for Europe offices in Brussels and Strasbourg over alleged misuse of parliament funds https://euobserver.com/244196/eu-prosecutors-raid-far-right-patriots-for-europe-offices-in-brussels-and-strasbourg-over-alleged-misuse-of-parliament-funds/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 20:02:50 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244196 The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) raided the offices of Patriots for Europe in Strasbourg and Brussels.]]> Offices of staff in the Patriots for Europe (PfE) group were raided in France and Belgium on Wednesday (21 October).

The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) told EUobserver that searches were carried out “as part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European funds by a former political group in the European Parliament”.

But the law enforcement body said it would not release details of the investigation for now, to avoid jeopardising the integrity of the case.

The far-right PfE group in the European Parliament, led by Jordan Bardella of the French National Rally (RN) party, posted a statement on social media claiming that on Wednesday morning, the EPPO carried out searches in administrative offices at the European Parliament premises in Brussels and Strasbourg.

“It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy Group (ID) dissolved in 2024,” said PfE’s X post.

]]> ‘Project Fear’ didn’t work, so why do we keep demonising far-right and left voters? https://euobserver.com/244150/project-fear-didnt-work-so-why-do-we-keep-demonising-far-right-and-left-voters/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244150 My beef with both far-right and far-left populists is that they're false prophets. In Europe, at least, the squeezes on public services, high taxes, debt burdens and crippling costs of living are legacies of the Covid pandemic, wars in Ukraine and Iran and a eurozone crisis that was never fully resolved. These can’t be wished away, and they won’t be cured with caps on immigration, higher taxes on the rich or the promise of earlier retirement.]]> Ten years ago, ‘Project Fear’ was at the heart of the ‘Remain’ campaign’s inept efforts to persuade Britons not to vote to leave the EU. 

Voting for Brexit, according to David Cameron’s government Doomsday forecasts, would cost every household £4,300 (€5,000) per year from 2030, lead to an immediate recession and mean lower house prices. 

It was a huge mistake. That all the pro-EU camp could say about being members of the club was that it would be very expensive to leave was a jarring admission of failure. And the promised economic apocalypse of instant recession and house price warnings didn’t happen. Most people simply didn’t believe the figures or that the politicians behind them were being honest about them. The result, as we know, is that more than 17m Brits gave the ‘establishment’ – or what they perceived it to be – a big kick up the arse. 

Fast forward to 2026 and newly-minted UK prime minister Andy Burnham has put all options for UK-EU relations – including rejoining – back on the table. 

The UK Treasury, which drew up the prophecies of doom, is now expected to publish a study analysing the potential economic benefits of Britain moving closer to the EU ahead of November’s EU-UK summit.

Personally, I think Brexit and the piecemeal trade and cooperation agreement that governs EU-UK trade has resulted in a small but significant economic hit.

The hope is that the treasury won’t promise milk, honey and gold-paved streets if the UK rejoins the EU or its single market.  

If over-promising increases the speed at which voters get disappointed with governments, the Brexit vote is proof that trying to frighten people is the fastest way to lose an election.

]]> EU looks to UK, Canada, and Japan to plug €70bn hole in funding for Ukraine’s 2027 war effort https://euobserver.com/244118/eu-looks-to-uk-canada-and-japan-to-plug-e70bn-hole-in-funding-for-ukraines-2027-war-effort/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:45:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244118 The EU is pressing allies, such as the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway to help close a €70bn shortfall in Ukraine’s funding for next year.]]> The EU is pressing allies, such as the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway, to help close a €70bn shortfall in Ukraine’s funding for next year, after president Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the war will cost €155bn in 2027.

EU Council president António Costa told MEPs in Strasbourg on Wednesday (21 October) that member states already provided 80 percent of external aid to Ukraine and “international partners must also step up their efforts”. 

“Our commitment to peace must go hand in hand with sustained pressure on the aggressor,” he also said, after meeting Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels last week.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen also told MEPs on Wednesday: “The war will not be decided on the frontline; the war will be decided in our political will, in whether we stand up for freedom and democracy and support our Ukrainian friends.” 

Zelensky’s €155bn figure refers to Ukraine’s total war-related spending in 2027, part of which Kyiv covers from its own budget.

But that still left a €70bn gap that Ukraine needed foreign partners to fill, as next year approached.

The EU has already agreed a €90bn loan covering 2026 and 2027, meant to meet two-thirds of Ukraine’s financing needs over that period.

The remaining third was supposed to come from other partners, but so far that money has been secured only for 2026, not for 2027.

    A government elected to repair democratic institutions has to accept restraints precisely when it can most easily avoid them: strengthening parliament even when it dominates it, protecting independent media when they attack the government, and creating institutions whose authority does not depend on proximity to the prime minister.

    ]]>         Europe’s €800bn defence borrowing hides a reality of every country buying on its own https://euobserver.com/243439/europes-e800bn-defence-spending-splurge-yet-its-a-sellers-market-if-the-eu-barely-borrows-together-and-buys-alone/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 11:06:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243439 In defence, the bigger the order, the longer the production line and the lower the cost of each unit. That is a big reason why Europe has long bought American, for price as much as for technology. Europe could match it by buying together and sharing out the work along the value chain.]]> Europe is supposed to be financing its defence together. It barely is.

    Of the €800bn announced under ReArm Europe in March 2025, €650bn is not common money. It is an estimate of the extra room governments get under the national escape clause to spend up to 1.5 percent of GDP more on defence for four years.

    Each country still pays for that spending itself.

    The room is also temporary: EU Commission simulations suggest that maintaining higher defence spending after 2028 could require additional annual fiscal adjustment of 0.25 to 0.4 percentage points of GDP from 2029.

    The other €150bn is SAFE, and it is loans, not grants.

    The EU borrows and lends the money on, and each country repays its share. Grants are small: €1.5bn from the European Defence Industry Programme for 2025-2027, plus the European Defence Fund for joint research.

    Not every country has used these tools, as Table 1 shows. The Netherlands and Sweden have used neither. Like Germany, which has taken only the clause, they can borrow at least as cheaply as the EU, so SAFE gets them nothing.

    France has taken SAFE but not the clause, to protect the credibility of its budget plans.

    Table 1. Who uses SAFE and the national escape clause

    Source: Council of the EU, European Commission. Data as of 17 October 2026. * Hungary: allocated €16.2bn, now requesting €5.4bn; still pending. ** Italy: the Commission backed its request on 8 October 2026; the Council has yet to decide.

    Where SAFE does matter is on the eastern flank. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can borrow the equivalent of five to eight percent of their GDP, and Poland almost five percent.

    Graph 1. SAFE loans as a share of GDP, by country (%)

    Source: Council of the EU, European Commission, Eurostat. SAFE loans only, as a share of 2025 GDP. Amounts approved by the Council, except Italy and Hungary (* revised requests of €8bn and €5.4bn, September 2026). Data as of 17 October 2026.

    That leaves private money.

    The European Investment Bank and the European Investment Fund are trying to bring in private investors, partly by removing the reputational stigma of financing defence.

    But defence is almost a monopsony: the state is nearly the only buyer. Without a clear flow of public orders, private investment will be hard to come by.

    So Europe barely borrows together. And it buys alone.

    ]]>         Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting https://euobserver.com/243677/generation-z-in-france-spain-and-albania-is-trapped-study-hard-stay-poor-live-with-your-parents-no-wonder-theyre-protesting/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:55:17 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243677 From under-resourced schools in France to Spain’s housing crisis and student protests in Albania, the immediate grievances differ. Yet they raise a common question: can young people turn education into secure work and an independent life?]]> In Paris, students have protested over shortages of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school buildings.

    In Spain, the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal — who died on 7 October — became a rallying point for housing protests.

    In Tirana, students joined wider demonstrations over education costs and corruption allegations.

    These are not parts of a single movement, and the protests do not have one common cause. But they bring into focus a shared challenge: whether young people can see a credible route from education to decent work, and from financial dependence to a life of their own. 

    France: school conditions shape the starting line

    Since September, French students have demonstrated over teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and deteriorating school buildings. Their demands concern more than the day-to-day running of schools. They also raise a question about equal opportunity: can public education give every student the tools to move forward, regardless of where they live or what their family can afford?

    The wider figures help explain why that question matters.

    In 2025, 25.5 percent of people aged 15–29 in France were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 24.2 percent across the EU, according to Eurostat.

    In August 2026, unemployment among under-25s stood at 20.6 percent, against 8.2 percent for the population as a whole. The corresponding EU rates were 15.4 percent and 6.1 percent.

    Read more

    The forgotten protests: empty shelves and blocked roads in southern Italy, ignored by the media, reveal neglect by Meloni and EU

    These figures do not show that school shortages cause youth unemployment. They do show how difficult the step from education into work remains for many young people and why well-resourced schools matter most in areas with the fewest opportunities.

    Housing can make that transition harder still. In Paris, one-in-two private tenants under 30 spends more than 51 percent of their income on rent. A Eurostat indicator also shows that 70 percent of 20–24-year-olds and 25 percent of 25–29-year-olds either live with their parents or are financially connected to their household. 

    France scored 66 out of 100 and ranked 27th of 182 countries in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index. The index measures perceptions of public-sector corruption, not the number of proven incidents. It does not explain the school protests, but it underlines why transparency and accountability matter when public services and resources are at stake.

    Spain: when housing delays independence

    Abascal’s eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for decades prompted demonstrations in several Spanish cities and renewed calls for stronger tenant protections. Her case was not a youth protest, but it put a human face on a housing crisis that also shapes whether younger people can leave home and build an independent life.

    In 2025, 67.1 percent of Spaniards aged 18–34 lived with at least one parent, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute.

    Among those living with a parent, 28.3 percent said they could not afford to rent. The average age at which young people left home was 30.2, compared with 26.3 across the EU, according to Eurostat.

    Housing pressure does not operate in isolation. In 2025, 27.6 percent of Spaniards aged 15–29 were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, above the EU rate of 24.2%.

    In August 2026, unemployment among under-25s was 22.7 percent, more than twice the overall rate of 10 percent. When joblessness is so much higher among the young and rent is beyond the reach of many, delayed independence cannot be reduced to personal preference.

    Spain scored 55/100 in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 49th of 182 countries. That score does not establish a link between corruption and housing protests. But when people are asking for effective action on housing, transparency over how decisions are made — and accountability for whether they work — are part of the debate.

    Albania: growth is not enough if young people see no path forward

    In October, students in Tirana protested over education costs and corruption allegations, joining a broader anti-government movement. Their participation brought education and young people’s prospects into a wider debate about living costs, employment and trust in public institutions.

    Albania’s official figures show that 19 percent of the population was at risk of relative poverty in 2025, while 31.2 percent experienced severe material and social deprivation, according to INSTAT. The two measures describe different aspects of hardship: one compares household income with the national poverty threshold; the other captures enforced inability to afford basic goods and activities.

    Young people also face a difficult entry into the labour market. The World Bank’s ILO-modelled estimates put overall unemployment at 10.9 percent in 2025, rising to 25.6 percent among 15–24-year-olds. The estimated average age of leaving the parental household seemed to be 30.9, compared with 26.3 in the EU, according to Eurostat’s dataset. Together, however, these indicators describe the hurdles between education, employment and independence.

    Albania scored 39/100 and ranked 91st of 182 countries in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index. The measure is not a count of actual cases, but corruption allegations are part of the protests themselves. That makes transparency, accountability and public trust more than abstract principles: they shape whether people believe institutions respond fairly to their concerns.

    Behind the statistics

    Behind the statistics are millions of young people struggling to turn their ambitions into reality. The obstacles reinforce one another: under-resourced schools can narrow choices, unemployment can delay financial independence, and high housing costs can prolong dependence on family.

    Across the EU, house prices rose by 55.4 percent and rents by 26.7 percent between 2010 and 2024, often outpacing income growth, according to Eurofound.

    That is why the response cannot be confined to one policy area. It means properly staffed and maintained schools, routes from education into decent work, more affordable and social housing, targeted help with rent, and stronger protections for tenants.

    Young people should also have a meaningful say in policies that shape their education, employment and housing.

    A strong welfare state and effective social protection can help ensure that a young person’s prospects are not determined solely by family income or place of birth. If a low-income family cannot support a young person’s move towards independence, financial dependence can pass from one generation to the next. Tackling that cycle is part of building social justice and societies in which young people can plan a future with greater confidence.

    The future will show whether today’s protests lead to lasting policies. The test will be whether young people can study, find decent work and afford a home without their prospects being set by the circumstances into which they were born.

    ]]>         International Criminal Court shortlisted for EU award as MEPs urge protection for its judges against Trump sanctions https://euobserver.com/243669/international-criminal-court-shortlisted-for-eu-award-as-meps-urge-protection-for-its-judges-against-trump-sanctions/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:02:17 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243669 The ICC was shortlisted for the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought alongside a Tanzanian opposition leader and jailed Iranian protesters. ]]> The International Criminal Court (ICC) has been shortlisted for the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, an annual human-rights award from the European Parliament.

    The announcement on Monday (19 October) comes after US president Donald Trump put his weight behind Israeli efforts to discredit the international judicial body by extending sanctions against it.

    The ICC issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes, as well as other senior Israeli officials and Hamas. The US then responded by targeting its judges by impeding their day-to-day activities such as banking.

    New sanctions against the court were announced by the US administration this month after the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge who wrote a UN report concluding Israel is committing ​genocide in Gaza.

    The ICC court labelled the move as an “assault on the rule of law” and called on countries to step up to protect it.

    Read more

    ‘Bullies cannot be appeased’: Pressure mounts on EU to shield ICC from new US sanctions

    Sakharov Prize finalists named 

    Members of the EU parliament’s foreign affairs committee shortlisted the ICC and its members for the Sakharov Prize.

    Named after the Soviet nuclear scientist dissident Andrei Sakharov, the award has been previously awarded to the likes of Iranian protest icon Mahsa Amini and to the Ukrainian people enduring Russia’s attacks.

    “We stand by the ICC and its officials, and we are committed to safeguarding its work,” said Yannis Maniatis, Greek MEP for the Socialists & Democrats group which nominated the ICC for the award. “If the aggressors become the victims, and if we stand by helplessly as international justice erodes, we risk allowing those who believe themselves above the law to prevail.”

    Tundu Lissu, a Tanzanian opposition figure in court for inciting the public to disrupt an election and facing the possibility of death row, is also a Sakharov Prize finalist. “There is no doubt about the political nature of his detention,” said David McAllister, MEP for the European People’s Party who co-nominated Lissu.

    Human oversight is essential, especially where AI systems decide on recruitment or workers’ assessment, she said.

    Next to innovation, labour rules needed to ensure “fair and transparent practices, respect for human workers’ rights … and effective social dialog,” said Roxana Mînzatu, the EU commissioner for employment.

    “This revolutionary technology has to be regulated” so that it “delivers for all,” Isabelle Schömann, the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) deputy general secretary had also said during a conference organised by the centre-left S&D group in the European Parliament on 14 October, commenting on the need for the Quality Jobs Act to curb AI.

    The draft Quality Jobs Act that the European Commission plans to present in December aims to update the long out of date 1989 and 1990 health and safety workplace rules.

    It would also protect subcontractors and create standards for working in heatwaves, becoming more frequent with climate change.

    EU legislators need to ensure minimum standards so that “neither jobs nor businesses are jeopardised” with extreme weather, Yolanda Díaz Pérez, the Spanish labour minister, said ahead of Monday’s debate.

]]> Après une escale à La Réunion l’année dernière, le Fundtruck a de nouveau posé ses valises dans l’océan Indien, en associant cette fois La Réunion et Mayotte au sein d’une même étape. Le 24 septembre, Maddyness a ainsi organisé une étape hybride depuis le siège de la BRED à Saint-Denis, permettant aux entrepreneuses et entrepreneurs des deux territoires de présenter leur projet dans les mêmes conditions que les candidats de l’Hexagone.

Une étape entre La Réunion et Mayotte

Huit startups réunionnaises et mahoraises étaient en lice pour décrocher leur place en finale. Comme à chaque étape du Fundtruck, les entrepreneurs disposaient de trois minutes pour pitcher leur projet, avant cinq minutes de questions face à un jury composé d’investisseurs et d’acteurs de l’écosystème.

Pour cette édition particulière, 16 membres du jury se sont mobilisés, sur place à La Réunion ou à distance, afin d’écouter et de challenger les différents projets. 

À l’issue des délibérations, c’est CapstonAI qui s’est imposée auprès du jury. Fondée par Greg Hanffou, la startup accompagne les entreprises pour améliorer leur visibilité dans les réponses générées par les principaux outils d’intelligence artificielle, comme ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude et Perplexity.

Faire rayonner les écosystèmes ultramarins

Cette étape a permis de mettre une nouvelle fois en lumière le dynamisme entrepreneurial de territoires encore éloignés des grands hubs de l’innovation métropolitains. 

L’étape 2026 a pu aussi compter sur le soutien de la BRED Banque Populaire, partenaire de cette escale, ainsi que de La French Tech La Réunion, Bpifrance, IVECO, Electra, CF Advisory et CF - Compagnie Fiduciaire, avec Manuel Biota.

CapstonAI rejoint désormais les autres lauréats de la saison et se prépare à représenter La Réunion et Mayotte lors de la Grande Finale du Fundtruck 2026. Celle-ci aura lieu le 26 novembre au siège de LCL.. La tournée, elle, se poursuit avec des nouvelles étapes en Île-de-France, en Belgique, puis à Bordeaux.

      <title>‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build America</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/21/trump-ice-construction-worker-deportation</link>
      <description><p>Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fate</p><p>Every morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.</p><p>Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/21/trump-ice-construction-worker-deportation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood</link>
      <description><p>As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner</p><p>‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.</p><p>Not just yet, judging by the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G0L8wTLaS8U">extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year</a>: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.</p><p>In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse.       <title>Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

    <item>
      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>
