<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 22 Oct 2026 08:50:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[What happens to our daughter’s trust fund at 18?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/what-happens-to-our-daughters-trust-fund-at-18/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/what-happens-to-our-daughters-trust-fund-at-18/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Q: Our wonderful daughter, who has a mild general learning delay and attends a special school, is about to turn 18. I’m struggling with the arrangements we need to put in place for her.

We have used the annual €3,000 small gift exemption for many years and the resulting fund is held in bare trust for her benefit.

We need guidance on how to transfer it to her in a way that best serves her. In our will, she will equally share our estate with her two siblings in time.

A: The parents have used the small gift exemption here to good effect. This is where anyone can give someone else €3,000 a year, tax-free. That’s a potential gift of €6,000 per calendar year from two parents without reducing a child’s lifetime Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) threshold.

This money has been accumulating in a bare trust for their daughter’s benefit.

Parents considering gifting money in this way should ensure the account is designated as a trust at the outset, says Greg Flanagan, solicitor, and partner at Lavelle Partners.

If it’s simply in a bank account in a parent’s name, Revenue may refuse to recognise it as being in trust for the child, he says. This will have tax implications.

Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says

The beneficiary of a bare trust is the true owner of the assets, says Catriona Coady, head of tax at Goodbody.

“The trustees merely hold and administer the assets until the beneficiary is legally entitled to take control of them, typically age 18 in the case of a child,” Coady explains.

“Some immediate practical steps these parents can take now are to review the bare trust arrangement, confirm the balance and investment ownership, and plan with their daughter how the account will operate when she turns 18.”

Depending on her needs and wishes, the family could consider a supported bank account, proportionate spending controls agreed with her, a decision-making assistance or co-decision-making agreement, and an enduring power of attorney made by her if she has the required capacity, says Coady.

The reader indicates that in time, her three children will inherit the parents’ estate in equal parts.

Using a discretionary trust may be particularly suitable for this future inheritance, Coady says.

Rather than leaving her a one-third share outright, the parents could revise their will so that her intended share passes to trustees who can apply the assets for her housing, care, education, therapies and wider support, while making controlled payments over time, according to Coady.

These trustees would have full discretion about when and how the daughter receives the money, so it is important that trustees are people who you trust.

Typically, the parents would write a “letter of wishes” to guide the trustees. Although the letter is not legally binding, it is an important guide to the parents’ intentions.

But the existing bare trust fund is different. As the daughter is already the beneficial owner, the parents cannot unilaterally transfer her money into a discretionary trust, Coady says.

“If, once she is 18, she has capacity to make this specific decision, she could choose to settle some or all of the fund into a new trust, but she should receive independent legal advice and understand that she would be giving up an unrestricted entitlement in favour of trustee discretion,” Coady adds.

Her agreement must be voluntary and properly informed. Having a mild learning delay does not of itself mean that someone lacks capacity.

“Capacity is presumed and is assessed in relation to the particular decision, with appropriate support,” Coady says.

All inheritance tax-free thresholds rise in the budget but no wider reforms

“If she lacks capacity to decide whether to place her existing property in a discretionary trust, her parents cannot simply consent on her behalf.”

Advice would be needed on the supported decision-making arrangements available under the assisted decision-making framework.

Any proposal that removes her existing absolute entitlement to the bare trust would require careful scrutiny, Coady says.

‘Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source’

Catriona Coady, Goodbody

Before any transfer to a discretionary trust is considered, the family should obtain professional advice to determine the legal, tax and social welfare implications of the daughter’s particular circumstances.

However, one of the major benefits of a discretionary trust created under her parents’ will is that for a child with additional needs, their entitlement to State supports such as social welfare, a medical card and disability benefits may be protected. These supports are means-tested.

While assets retained in a discretionary trust are not generally owned by the child, any money or assets paid or appointed to her could become her income or capital and may affect her eligibility for means-tested support.

Get advice before distributions are made, Coady advises.

A discretionary trust is normally subject to tax of 6 per cent of the capital value of the trust fund in year one, and 1 per cent of the capital value for each year afterwards, for as long as the trust continues. If the beneficiary has additional needs and the trust is set up exclusively for them, a discretionary trust tax exemption may apply.

To qualify, Revenue usually requires a medical report or letter from a doctor confirming the child is incapable of managing their own affairs, says Flanagan.

Can I avoid capital gains tax on a rental property by gifting it to my child?

When assets are eventually distributed or appointed out of the trust to a beneficiary, standard gift or inheritance tax rules and thresholds still apply at a rate of 33 per cent on amounts above the child’s €420,000 tax-free threshold, regardless of disability, Flanagan says.

However, depending on the nature and purpose of a payment from the trust, it may be CAT exempt – for example, where funds are used for the beneficiary’s qualifying support and maintenance, or for qualifying expenses related to medical care.

Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source, so specific tax advice should be taken, Coady says.

The parents might also want to consider the dwelling house exemption – this would allow their daughter to receive the parents’ main home, lived in until the time of their death, tax-free if certain conditions are met, Flanagan says.

If the daughter has occupied this as her main home three years before the date of inheritance, and will continue to do so for at least six years after, and she doesn’t have an interest in another residential property at the date of inheritance or the valuation date – in her own right or in her parents’ will – she could inherit the property tax-free.

The name of the reader who submitted the question is not being published to protect the identities of those involved.

]]><![CDATA[Meta ordered to pay $25bn in New Mexico, faces new class action in Australia]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/22/meta-ordered-to-pay-25bn-in-new-mexico-faces-new-class-action-in-australia/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/22/meta-ordered-to-pay-25bn-in-new-mexico-faces-new-class-action-in-australia/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:22:34 +0000A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion (€22.24 billion) after a jury ‌found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.

The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved ​in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.

Mathew found that a penalty of ​more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.

In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, ⁠makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to ‌enforce ‌new ​rules for what people can say online.”

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement after the ruling that the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.

Meta is also facing a class-action lawsuit in Australia that alleges its Instagram and Facebook social media platforms exposed ​children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms.

The lawsuit, filed in Australia’s second-highest court by law firm MinterEllison ​this month, could be the first in Australia to blame social media ⁠for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers. It was filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed ⁠by Meta while ​they were under the age of ​18, and are seeking compensation.

Separately, Meta signalled it was getting ready to bet more aggressively on the AI market, with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg telling investors that a pricey wager on artificial intelligence is delivering results.

]]><![CDATA[Workplace conflict costs millions annually, but what can be done to remedy this problem?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:56:00 +0000When I moved here from New York more than three decades ago, I became the default complainer in restaurants. It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”

If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?

As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.

Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.

William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.

“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.

Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicate that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euros in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.

The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.

Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.

Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.

Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.

When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.

Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.

Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.

“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”

Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.

She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.

Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”

Managing conflict: Top tips:

1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;

2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;

3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;

4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;

5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

  • Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

It would be easy to shrug and say that people should always have a backup. A second bank card with a different financial institution; perhaps some emergency cash just in case (did none of us read the Government’s emergency booklet?) to get us through.

There but for the grace of the tech gods go all of us. The problem wasn’t down to Revolut’s systems, or a cyberattack, but a failure at Google Cloud. The company has made a concerted push into the financial services market as it vies for business with rivals Microsoft and AWS.

It could have been any bank; this time, it just happened to be Revolut, a relative newcomer to the banking world that is still treated dismissively by some. This is despite the fact that more than 3 million people in Ireland use the digital bank’s services. A good number of those users were lured away from Ireland’s traditional banks, which have been forced to provide better digital services to customers.

And it wasn’t just Revolut that was affected. Although AIB and Bank of Ireland reported no problems with their services, in the UK, Lloyds and HSBC also suffered the effects of the outage. The UK’s courts video system was taken down too.

Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland?

The issue that Revolut’s outage raised is not that we should turn away from digital banks; it is the fact that we are overly dependent on a small number of tech systems in every facet of our daily lives. Take out one and the cascade effect is terrifying to behold.

These incidents are relatively rare, but they happen. Ironically, it was a year to the day that a big problem with AWS’s services caused apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat to go dark. That was followed only days later by a Microsoft Azure issue, an “inadvertent configuration change” that not only knocked Microsoft’s own services offline, but also affected airlines, Heathrow airport and even An Post.

They are, in a way, a victim of their own success. If Google, Microsoft, and AWS were not supporting as many of the day-to-day services we use, we wouldn’t notice if the service had a minor blip. But they do and, consequently, when things go wrong, the impact is widespread.

It is not just the infrastructure underpinning these services that is out of our hands. A French judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Nicolas Guillou, found that his access to many of the services we take for granted has been effectively blocked after US president Donald Trump imposed sanctions on him. Travel bookings made through Expedia have been cancelled. His bank account has been restricted, and booking flights or other transport is almost impossible for him.

Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?

The sanctions, which were imposed on a number of ICC judges and block US entities and their overseas subsidiaries from providing services to him, came following investigations into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan and Palestine and the issuing of arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?

More recently, the reported slowdown of Starlink’s satellite communications system in Ukraine affected the country’s ability to defend itself. Ukraine relies on the system to help intercept Russian missile and drone attacks; speed limits that were imposed last week made that a more difficult task.

According to the Wall Street Journal, that slowdown came at the order of billionaire Elon Musk. Musk appeared to point the finger at the White House, but the US has denied involvement.

Regardless of who was responsible, the end result was the same: a powerful billionaire somewhere put a thumb on the scale and ordinary people suffered the consequences.

These incidents all highlight our precarious position in Europe. Whether it is a concentration of business in a small number of tech firms or the shifting geopolitical landscape, Europe needs to get some sort of control over things.

Proposals published by the European Commission in June set a number of targets to help achieve this, from increasing data centre capacity to supporting chip production. Bureaucracy moves slowly, though, and EU bureaucracy is a particular behemoth. The targets set are still a good way off, and Europe is starting from behind.

The alternative, though, is throwing up our hands and giving up. To adapt a phrase, the best time to start developing tech sovereignty was yesterday; the second best time is now.

Europe needs alternatives, and it needs them fast.

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.

A new Government website will make it easier for you to find out.

Ireland’s national gender pay gap stands at 8.3 per cent, according to figures quoted by the Department of Equality this year. That’s the average difference in pay between all men and all women in the workforce. If you’re a woman working in an organisation on the wrong side of the gap, it pays to know about it.

New data published from next month aims to lift the lid on gaps in pay and equip you to find out how your workplace measures up.

New portal

By the end of November, all employers with more than 50 employees must publish data about their gender pay gap to a new public gender pay gap portal.

The gender pay gap is the average difference in pay between all men and all women in an organisation. If you are a woman working in an organisation where there is a big gap, it doesn’t bode well for your finances.

The pay portal has been open for voluntary reporting since last year and viewable to the public since June, but publication by employers is about to become mandatory.

The Employment Equality Bill 2026 will be enacted in the coming weeks, with individual company gender pay gap figures for 2026 available to view by the end of November, Minister for Equality Norma Foley told the Dáil last week.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) put Ireland’s national gender pay gap at 9.6 per cent in 2022. Mean hourly earnings for men were €27.73 and €25.06 for women, a gap of €2.67.

As age increases, the gender pay gap grows. The biggest gap was in the 50-59 age group at 16.7 per cent, with men earning €33.03 and women earning €27.51.

Sectors such as construction, aviation and finance tend to show wider gaps due to male-dominated senior roles, while education and healthcare often show the opposite trend.

In many cases, it’s less about pay rates and more about representation at senior levels, says UCD’s Professional Academy.

It’s important to note the gender pay gap is not a test of whether men and women in an organisation are paid equally for the same work – that’s already required by law. Rather, it highlights imbalances that influence how opportunities are distributed, according to the academy.

If your organisation has a big gender pay gap, there may be some telltale signs.

There are probably fewer women in senior or higher-paid roles; there is an over-representation of women in lower-paid or part-time roles in a company; maybe there is unconscious bias or barriers to the progression of women; there is a culture where availing of hybrid working is frowned on; or maybe there is a culture where the men who work there never take leave for caring responsibilities.

Female participation in Irish workforce jumps 90% since 2000

Some or all of these characteristics can contribute to a workplace where pay between genders is out of whack.

If you work in or are interviewing for a role in an organisation with a big pay gap, the impact can ripple far beyond your pay cheque.

Lower average pay than male colleagues in an organisation can mean women there get a smaller percentage pay rise than male colleagues, receive a less generous pay-linked bonus, are unable to borrow as much their male colleagues can to buy a house, and end up with smaller pensions in retirement.

If you are already in a job or scouting for a new one, the new pay gap portal will make it easier to look under the bonnet and see the reality of the hiring, pay, promotion practices and culture there.

Scores on the doors

Gender pay gap reporting requires employers to choose a snapshot day in June this year, and use pay information for the previous 12 months for their pay gap calculations. Employers then have five months to publish their report, by the end of November.

Some 1,000 employers have now created accounts on the portal in preparation for publishing their reports by the end of next month, the Department of Equality says.

Some firms have been proactive, voluntarily publishing their 2025 pay gap data to the portal. You’ll find 410 such reports already published.

Searching the portal by company name and looking for the mean, or average gender pay gap, is a useful metric for employees, says Michelle McDonagh, chief client officer at human resource management consultancy Adare.

If you see a large gender pay gap percentage, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the organisation is paying women unfairly, says McDonagh.

“Gender pay gap measures the pay of all men and compares it against all women. There is no allowance for the type of role, length of service, level of seniority or expertise,” she says.

“It’s a blunt instrument in that regard.”

The gender pay gap figure, however, is a useful indicator of hiring and promotion practices, policies and culture in a company.

Being a working mother is a horror show at times. The stress can be crippling

A zero per cent pay gap is the ideal. That would mean men and women’s pay is perfectly balanced.

A positive gender pay gap, of five per cent for example, means women earn five per cent less on average than men. A negative, or minus gap, means men earn less than women on average.

“Most organisations will have a positive figure because in most organisations, women will earn less than men on average,” says McDonagh.

Comparing companies by sector can provide an interesting perspective.

Take the telecommunications, computer programming and consulting sector in the data, for example. This is one of the most highly remunerated sectors in the country. Consultancy firm Deloitte has been proactive in publishing its data and reports a 5.2 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in favour of men.

Another useful search in the portal is “distribution of gender by pay quartile”. This requires bosses to segment their workforce by pay band and tell you the balance of men and women in each of four different bands. Looking at Deloitte, there were 10 per cent more women than men in the lower middle pay band in 2025, but 4 per cent more men than women in the very top pay band.

“One of the trends we tend to see in companies is if there are a lot of females coming into lower-paid roles and for whatever reason they are not progressing through the ranks,” says McDonagh.

“Then you see a lot of males in the higher-paid roles and women’s representation drops away as they move through those different pay quartiles.”

What top CEO pay and gender pay gap reporting tell us about Irish business

Companies are required to publish a statement about what is causing their pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Deloitte’s statement says the company has met its target of 35 per cent female partners by 2025.

“We aim to increase this to 40 per cent by 2027, with a 50 per cent longer-term goal,” according to the firm.

Data for PwC shows a 1.6 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in the mean hourly pay of female and male employees.

Women and men are 50:50 in the lowest pay quartile, but there are 10 per cent more women than men in the topmost pay quartile.

‘Women make up at least half of our population. This, in turn, has had a significant influence on the outcome of our gender pay gap analysis,” says PwC.

KPMG, Ernst & Young (EY) or Accenture have not published data on the portal for 2025. They will be required to publish their 2026 data by the end of November.

They were required to publish 2025 pay gap data on their own websites, however.

KPMG reports an average gender pay gap of 11.1 per cent for 2025 – the organisation comprises 51 per cent women and 49 per cent men. There are more women than men in all three lower pay quartiles, but 11 per cent more men at the top pay quartile.

There is a 23.2 per cent average bonus gap between men and women at the consulting firm, its report says.

At partner level, women represent 24 per cent of partners. The pay gap between female and male partners is 5.6 per cent.

Pay transparency rules could cause conflict in workplaces, say HR and law experts

The mean pay gap at Accenture for 2025 is 9.2 per cent. The number of women and men are almost equal in all pay quartiles – except at the top one where there are 10 per cent more men in the highest pay grade.

The mean pay gap at EY for 2025 is 6.5 per cent. Some 71 per cent of partners are male.

Meta Platforms Ireland, which employs 95 per cent of Meta’s staff here, has a 2025 gender pay gap of 26.5 per cent, and an average bonus pay gap of 37 per cent.

The company employs an almost equal number of men and women. The number of women at Meta is greatest in its lowest pay quartile, where there are 62 per cent women, and the number of women is fewest in the highest pay quartile, where there are 63 per cent men.

Women are better represented in non-tech roles in the company, Meta says. Tech roles, like software engineers, are typically paid more in the market, and this has a disproportionate impact on pay gaps, it says.

The bonus gap is higher than the hourly pay gap, which is primarily driven by higher tech equity, it says.

Hooke & MacDonald is the only large real estate firm to have voluntarily published its gender pay gap data to the Government portal for 2025. It reports a 13 per cent gender pay gap in the mean hourly pay of female employees and of male employees.

“We are clear that our pay gap arises as a result of a greater proportion of males in senior positions in specific areas of the business and on higher pay points within those grades – due to longer service in those roles. This significantly contributes to the pay gap,” the company says.

This is down to a relatively higher share of roles taken up by women in administrative grades, which have a lower average hourly pay than other grades, it says.

There are 8 per cent more women than men in the second-from-top pay band, but 12 per cent more men in the top band.

“A great deal of effort [is being made] in recent years to improve our gender balance at senior manager level, including actively supporting family-friendly initiatives such as hybrid working, work sharing, statutory leave schemes and the shorter working year scheme,” says the commission.

The commission reported its 2025 pay gap in three categories – men, women and non-binary – but says the format of the portal makes it impossible to fully report on pay gap statistics for the three groups.

An Post reports a zero gender pay gap for the fifth consecutive year. Its 2025 data shows a mean hourly gender pay gap of minus 4.85 per cent in favour of women. It has an equal percentage of male and female executive directors.

Banking and finance sectors slow to disclose salary information, data shows

Perception

Gender pay gap stats may be particularly beneficial to women in the middle pay quartile, says McDonagh.

“If you can see the norm in your company is for more male representation at the top, maybe you hadn’t realised that’s the context you are working in – the report will tell you that,” says McDonagh.

“Then you are going to have to take charge of your own career, you are going to have to drive it yourself.

“If the stats tell you that men in your organisation have the majority of the income, you are going to have to drive those conversations with your manager yourself to make sure you are getting the opportunity to progress. Keep asking the question, what do I have to do to move up?”

The data is a very public opening of the kimono for organisations, and at a time when HR headcount and diversity and inclusion initiatives are under fire.

“Some 64 per cent of employers have identified employee perception as their biggest concern about publication of their gender pay gap report,” says Adare’s McDonagh of her company’s most recent HR Barometer data.

While gender pay gap statistics can be a bit of a blunt instrument, the statement employers are required to publish explaining the data can be insightful, says McDonagh.

This self-examination requires them to explain the cause of their gender pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Work to transpose the remaining parts of the European Union (EU) Pay Transparency Directive is continuing, the department says. This will include the obligation for employers to carry out a gender-neutral job evaluation. This requires employers to examine why they are remunerating some types of work more than others. It involves assessing the value of different types of work in their organisation, putting work of similar value into the same category and ensuring these people are similarly paid.

This means equal pay for those doing work of the same value too – even if that work looks quite different.

In UK clothing retailer Next, for example, the mostly female sales staff were found to be earning less than the company’s mostly male warehouse workers. Even though their jobs seem different, the retail staff contributed work of equal value to the warehouse workers, a tribunal found.

Employers will be invited to training to help them compare work objectively – based on skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions – to eliminate gender pay gaps and bias.

Done right, this could upend old pay structures that have unfairly rewarded some skills over others, for no objective reason.

]]><![CDATA[Why developers are turning to hotels, not apartments]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The cracks are starting to show. After years of defying reality about the Dublin office market’s prospects, developers are now embracing the hotel market as never before.

The latest convert is the German property group KGAL, which wants to knock down an office block on Dublin’s Golden Lane and build a 225-bedroom hotel. They follow in the footsteps of Core Capital’s Derek McGrath and of Johnny Ronan’s eponymous property group, both of which have reversed planned office developments.

The change of heart reflects an anaemic market for office space in Dublin, with CBRE expecting the take-up of office space this year to be roughly in line with last year but below the long-run average. They see a few bright spots on the horizon and tentative signs of the new development cycle, helped somewhat counter-intuitively by demand from artificial intelligence companies.

A more downbeat view is expressed by Peter Keegan, the director of debt and structured finance at CBRE, in a letter submitted to Dublin City Council as part of the KGAL planning application. It can be paraphrased as saying that, notwithstanding the green shoots mentioned above, lenders are wary of office development in Dublin.

Or, as Keegan put it, “there will be much deeper liquidity from debt providers for the development of a hotel on the site versus a new office building ... this is a development which will be received more positively as a hotel project than a speculative office scheme”.

Lenders call the shots in property development, and their enthusiasm for hotel projects is easy to understand. There is a well-documented shortage of hotel rooms in the capital, as evidenced by high occupancy rates. The shortfall is put at 3,600 beds, which equates to 20 or so hotels along the lines of the one planned by KGAL.

The downside with hotels is you have to find someone to run it for you, but if you can get more than 80 per cent occupancy, you will do well. It’s not a one-way bet. About 2,600 new beds are already in the pipeline, according to consultants Mitchell McDermott. The window of opportunity is closing and hence the stampede towards hoteliership by office developers.

From this perspective, their lack of enthusiasm for building apartments is hard to understand given the much larger and open-ended demand – 50,000 homes a year for the foreseeable future.

Again, the KGAL planning application is instructive. It contains an assessment of the site’s potential for an apartment development. The planning report argues that if the various rules and regulations pertaining to apartments – such as access to daylight and minimum open spaces – were to be complied with, then the maximum number of apartments that could be built on the site is between 50 and 60 units. This would not be “viable” even though it is a 10-minute walk from Grafton Street.

The site’s suitability for student accommodation is also deemed not to be “viable”. Urbanest, the student accommodation provider, kindly supplied a letter saying planning constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable. Two-hundred bed spaces would be needed.

Viability gets mentioned a lot in the KGAL planning application, but it is not really defined. Presumably what they are talking about is commercial viability and that is something of movable feast.

It takes a lot of factors into account, including the value of the site for other uses, the costs of construction and the availability and cost of debt financing. It also includes opportunity cost – whether you might make more money using the debt and resources required for Golden Lane elsewhere.

Viability is thus not the same thing as profitability. It may well be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane, but just not as profitable as building a hotel.

Whether it is “viable” to choose an option that delivers a lower profit is another question entirely. It is perfectly reasonable for KGAL to argue it is not viable for them to choose an option – such as apartments instead of a hotel – that will deliver a lower return to their investors.

But that does not mean it would not be viable for someone else with access to cheaper funding and different objectives, such as the Land Development Agency, to build apartments.

Dublin city planners would be doing us some service if they looked a little deeper into the question of viability. Is KGAL saying it would not be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane or simply that it would be more profitable to build a hotel?

The planners might then apply their own definition of viability. It would seem axiomatic that if a 60-unit apartment development could be built at a profit, it would be more than viable from the perspective of the Government’s obligation to house people.

]]><![CDATA[Keelings seeking occupiers for latest phase at FoodCentral business park]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/keelings-seeking-occupiers-for-latest-phase-at-foodcentral-business-park/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/keelings-seeking-occupiers-for-latest-phase-at-foodcentral-business-park/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:45:00 +0000Keelings, the well-known family-owned Irish food business, has engaged Finnegan Menton and Cushman & Wakefield as joint sale and letting agents for the latest phase of lands at FoodCentral, the 280-acre food industry park it owns at St Margaret’s near Dublin Airport. Rental levels for completed buildings, meanwhile, will depend on specification and the overall building and plot size. A range of options are available to prospective occupiers including design and build or lease.

The launch of the latest sites at FoodCentral comes as Dixon Transport nears the completion of the fourth phase of development at its facility since locating there in 2015. The latest phase comprises a fully automated ambient and temperature-controlled distribution centre of 10,200sq m (110,000sq ft) immediately adjoining a slightly larger sized facility completed in mid-2024. Dixon’s facilities at FoodCentral will extend to more than 28,000sq m (300,000sq ft) once the current works are completed.

Derry Group Ireland acquired a 5.7-acre site at FoodCentral in late 2024 and secured planning permission within three months for a new 2,046sq m (22,000sq ft) refrigerated warehouse and truck parking facility. The development is due for completion by the end of this year. Derry Group specialises in the storage, order picking and distribution of chilled and frozen products throughout Ireland with depots in Armagh, Dublin and Cork.

French investor pays €15m for Portlaoise logistics facility

A Tesla Supercharger station is also under construction at FoodCentral with eight superchargers being delivered in the current phase, with another six spaces to follow in phase two. Keelings Farm Shop and Cafe is also set for expansion, with planning permission recently granted by Fingal County Council to extend the existing space to more than 416sq m (4,480sq ft).

The FoodCentral scheme is well located immediately next to the northern runway at Dublin Airport, and about a six-minute drive from the M1, M2 and M50 motorways. Dublin Port Tunnel is about a 10-minute drive away.

Nicholas Corson of Finnegan Menton said discussions were already under way with a number of parties in relation to the sale of sites and for the development of completed buildings within FoodCentral. A plot of 5.5 acres within the 41 acres now being marketed is already reserved and at legals.

Brendan Smyth of Cushman & Wakefield said: “FoodCentral is an excellent location for both processing and logistics. The scheme is close to Dublin Airport and the road network and offers prospective occupiers flexibility in regard to site size, scale and future expansion.”

]]><![CDATA[Leixlip town centre site with scope for 48 apartments guiding at €1.75m ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/leixlip-town-centre-site-with-scope-for-48-apartments-guiding-at-175m/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/leixlip-town-centre-site-with-scope-for-48-apartments-guiding-at-175m/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:40:00 +0000Developers and investors involved in the delivery of housing for the owner-occupier, private rented sector and student accommodation markets are expected to run the rule over the sale of a prominent property and site in the heart of Leixlip town in Co Kildare.

Shingle House, a distinctive three-storey period building of 258sq m (2,777sq ft), which occupies a 0.5-hectare (1.24-acre) site at the junction of Leixlip Road and Main Street, is being offered to the market by agent Lisney Commercial Real Estate at a guide price of €1.75 million.

The subject property and its site are zoned for the most part as Zone A – Town Centre under the terms of the Leixlip Local Area Plan (LAP) 2020 – 2023, as extended to March 2029. The property is also included in Leixlip’s Town Centre Regeneration Area.

In the case of Intel, its Leixlip campus is its largest European manufacturing and innovation base and has been in operation since 1989.

For those parties interested in exploring the site’s potential for student accommodation, Shingle House is situated 10.6km from Maynooth University.

]]><![CDATA[‘Lessons learned’ as Kelly family scales back plans for housing scheme in south Dublin]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/lessons-learned-as-kelly-family-scales-back-plans-for-housing-scheme-in-south-dublin/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/lessons-learned-as-kelly-family-scales-back-plans-for-housing-scheme-in-south-dublin/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000A housing development proposed on the site of two cottages in south Co Dublin has been significantly scaled back after a previous planning application was thrown out and the project was held up in the appeals process for nearly two years.

The initial plans were deemed to constitute “overdevelopment” of the area, between Foxrock and Blackrock, although the team behind the project says the renewed proposal “is heavily informed [by] lessons learned” from its past experience.

Developer Kelland Homes has applied for permission to construct 22 houses and apartments in blocks up to three storeys tall on a site facing the Clonkeen Road in Deansgrange, documents filed last week to Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council show.

The developer spent more than €2.5 million in total through two purchases more than five years apart from one another, to acquire the site that consists of two two-bedroom bungalow cottages and amounts to a little over a quarter of a hectare in size.

Kelland’s new application has reduced the number of planned units by more than a third. The developer previously sought to construct 35 apartments in blocks up to six storeys tall, planning records from nearly four years ago show.

The local council rejected the initial proposal in April 2022, with its planning office stating the “overall scale, height and form” of the development would be “detrimental” to the surrounding properties. Its “visually overbearing” stature would “unreasonably compromise” the local area, planning documents read.

An appeal was lodged in May 2022 by Kelland Homes, which was established in the 1970s by Patrick Kelly, the well-known Celtic Tiger-era property tycoon. The company is still largely owned by Kelly’s family.

Rise and fall of a Tiger tycoon

In January 2024, nearly two years after the planning application was submitted, An Bord Pleanála (now known as An Coimisiún Pleanála) upheld the council’s decision.

The State planning authority said the plans “would constitute overdevelopment” and “would seriously injure the residential and visual amenities of property in the vicinity of the site”.

In supporting documents submitted last week to the council, a town planning consultancy firm working on behalf of Kelland Homes said that the “revised proposals” are “substantially different” from the original development and its volume has been “significantly reduced”.

The developer is now seeking permission to construct 10 town houses of three or four bedrooms and 10 apartments of two or three bedrooms, not exceeding three storeys in height, the renewed planning application reads.

The site currently hosts two semidetached bungalows, which Kelland Homes proposes to partially demolish and later refurbish. The two properties sit on a combined 0.43 hectares, according to data from Tailte Éireann, which maintains the State’s official land register.

One of the homes, 21 Monaloe Cottages, was sold in October 2020 for €1,625,000, while the adjoining 20 Monaloe Cottages property was sold in April 2026 for €900,000, according to the Property Price Register. Both cottages had two bedrooms at the time of their sale.

Kelland Homes also proposes “the relocation of the existing bus shelter and associated bus stop on Clonkeen Road”, which services the Dublin Bus L26 route to Blackrock Dart station, to provide space for the development’s entrance.

]]>Frank_U<![CDATA[State’s population surges by almost 800,000 in a decade]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/states-population-surges-by-almost-800000-in-a-decade/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/states-population-surges-by-almost-800000-in-a-decade/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 15:21:37 +0000The State’s population has risen by almost 800,000 in the last decade, with two-thirds of the increase coming from net inward migration.

Figures indicate that the Republic’s population grew by 786,000 or 16.6 per cent between 2016 and 2026 to stand at 5.5 million.

This was the third highest increase in the European Union behind Malta and Luxembourg. It compares to an overall EU population increase of less than 2 per cent.

The Central Statistics Office said the Republic’s population growth was driven by positive net migration and by a natural increase as a result of more births than deaths.

Net migration – the difference between the number of people moving to and from the State – totalled 511,000 since 2016, which accounted for 65 per cent of the overall increase in population here.

“Over the last 10 years, Ireland has consistently recorded positive net migration,” the CSO said.

“However, net migration in 2026 fell by 19.4 per cent (to 48,100) compared with the previous year. Net migration peaked at 79,300 in 2024,” it said.

The agency’s latest Measuring Ireland’s Progress report noted that over the last 10 years the natural increase in the population (births minus deaths) has almost halved, from 35,600 in 2016 to 18,800 in 2026.

During the period, the proportion of the population aged 45 and over rose from 37.1 per cent to 42.2 per cent, whereas the proportion aged under 45 fell from 62.9 per cent to 57.8 per cent.

In 2025, Ireland also had the highest young-age dependency ratio in the EU at 28.1 per cent. This ratio measures the number of children aged under 15 years as a proportion of the “working-age population” aged 15-64.

The State also had the second lowest old-age dependency ratio (the number of people aged 65 or over as a proportion of those aged 15-64) in the EU at 23.8 per cent.

With households in the grip of another inflationary surge, the CSO’s report also noted Ireland had the second-highest price level for consumer goods and services in the EU in 2025 at 36.2 per cent above the EU average, while Denmark had the highest at 39.7 per cent above average.

The figures also indicated that the State’s national debt has fallen to its lowest level since the banking crisis began in 2008.

Total debt fell to just under €210 billion last year, equating to 63 per cent of modified gross national income (GNI*), the agency’s bespoke measure of national income here.

In the wake of the banking bailouts post-2008, Ireland’s debt as a percentage of GNI* soared to 166 per cent.

The State’s improved debt picture since then stands in stark contrast to the trend internationally, with debt crises engulfing several countries, most notably France, the United States and the United Kingdom.

France’s debt – at €3.6 trillion – is currently 120 per cent of the country’s income. The worsening trajectory of its annual fiscal deficit has triggered a surge in French bond yields, hiking up the annual cost of servicing its debt.

Ireland’s debt-to-GDP ratio has been helped more by the rise in national income rather than a reduction in the debt itself.

The State’s GDP has doubled to €602.4 billion since 2015 on the back of huge multinational-led investment.

As a percentage of GDP, Ireland’s debt was 32.9 per cent last year, the fifth-lowest government debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU.

However, it still equated to €37,988 for every person in the State, which is large by international standards.

CSO’s figures also indicated that Ireland recorded the highest annual GDP growth rate within the EU, at 8 per cent.

This represented a reversal from 2023, when Ireland experienced the lowest GDP growth rate in the EU, at -3.3 per cent.

The market extended ⁠Monday’s rebound, as investors bought the dip in technology stocks following last week’s bruising sell-off, fuelled in part by concerns over ‌CoreWeave’s debt ‌load ​and the cost of financing the AI buildout.

“You’re seeing ⁠some strength in some high-value stocks and the Dow, ​and so that’s helping to sort of lift the overall indexes,” said ​Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Christophe Ena<![CDATA[Live commerce platform Whatnot to double Irish workforce in 18 months]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/live-commerce-platform-whatnot-to-double-irish-workforce-in-18-months/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/live-commerce-platform-whatnot-to-double-irish-workforce-in-18-months/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 17:08:23 +0000Live commerce platform Whatnot is to double its Irish workforce in the next 18 months as it expands its European headquarters in Dublin.

]]><![CDATA[Millions affected by Revolut disruption linked to Google Cloud outage]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:33:03 +0000Millions of customers of digital bank Revolut found themselves unable to access financial services after a power outage at Google Cloud caused widespread disruption on Tuesday.

Customers across Ireland and the UK reported problems accessing the bank’s systems, from logging in to the app and transferring funds, to making card payments and cash withdrawals.

The disruption was linked to an outage at Google Cloud, which provides core infrastructure services to Revolut.

The problems began early on Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours, with Downdetector recording a spike in reports between 7 and 8am. Revolut confirmed the outage, but moved to reassure customers that their data and money had not been compromised.

“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” a spokesman said. “We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

Revolut customers in Ireland affected by ‘third-party’ data breach

Revolut has 3.4 million customers in Ireland.

Google later confirmed the problem was caused by a “power event” at Google Cloud’s “Europe-west2-b” region, which knocked services offline early on Tuesday morning and caused intermittent network failures.

“A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated,” Google said. It later updated customers, saying the issue with impacted products had been reduced for most of those affected. “It is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our engineering team is working on it.”

Revolut was not the only company affected. In the UK, Lloyds Bank and HSBC users were also reporting issues to Downdetector, as well as DPD and the courts video platform used throughout the country.

AIB and Bank of Ireland said they were unaffected, and that all services were operating normally.

Google’s cloud division is competing with rivals Microsoft and AWS in providing cloud services to critical industries. This outage has brought the reliance of companies on a small number of cloud services back into the spotlight.

In October last year, a problem with AWS took down major apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat, along with banks, transport and messaging services. That was followed a week later by an issue at Microsoft Azure after an “inadvertent configuration change” caused problems for users.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Paddy Power owner Flutter to cut 240 jobs at Irish head office]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 12:18:58 +0000Paddy Power owner Flutter will cut 240 jobs from its Irish head office as it grapples with rising British betting taxes.

The group said on Tuesday that it planned to cut about 1,400 jobs in its UK and Ireland division to counter the impact of British government tax rises set to cost it $540 million (€480 million).

About 240 of those jobs will be lost in its Dublin office, while the group will also reduce numbers in the United Kingdom and in various centres around Europe, according to sources familiar with the business.

Flutter did not comment on the numbers that will be lost in each location.

However, an industry source estimated that up to 550 jobs could go in the UK, with the remaining cuts in Porto, Portugal, and Cluj-Napoca, Romania, Malta and Gibraltar, which service the UK and Ireland division.

Along with Paddy Power, the unit includes Betfair and Sky Bet.

Gaming and betting duty hikes announced by Britain’s Labour government will cost Flutter’s UK and Ireland unit $540 million this year, the group has already confirmed.

Its business in the Republic is suffering as it forms part of the UK and Ireland division, where the impact of the tax increases will be felt.

UK and Ireland chief executive Kevin Harrington said the group was not able to “fully absorb” this without cutting costs.

Paddy Power’s long goodbye from betting shops accelerates

Plans announced in last year’s UK autumn budget noted the rate of remote gaming duty – the tax on online casino games and slots – increased from 21 per cent to 40 per cent earlier this year.

Firms will also see a new 25 per cent rate of general betting duty for online bets from April next year, up from 15 per cent, as part of the budget changes.

Flutter employs 1,750 people in its Irish office in Clonskeagh, Dublin and 9,000 overall in the UK and Ireland division.

The group plans to begin consultations with its Irish workers shortly. Local management told them of the planned cuts before the group announced the move on Tuesday morning.

Flutter recently confirmed plans to close up to 100 Paddy Power bookie shops in Ireland and Britain in light of growing economic uncertainty.

Its latest announcement comes as speculation grows that British prime minister Andy Burnham’s government could increase taxes on fruit, roulette and other slot machines in British bookie shops at the next budget later this month.

Such a move could spark further betting shop closures in Britain. The Republic’s laws do not permit those machines in bookies.

Flutter said its cost-cutting plan is likely to cost between $80 million (€71 million) and $90 million over the next three months.

Harrington said: “The material increase in betting and gaming duties announced in the UK budget last year has fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market.

“As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future.

“We remain confident that we are well placed to benefit from share gains given our position as the largest-scale operator in the UK.” – Additional reporting: PA

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Ryanair chief Michael O’Leary predicts 20% increase in airfares next year]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/ryanair-chief-michael-oleary-predicts-20-increase-in-air-fares-next-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/ryanair-chief-michael-oleary-predicts-20-increase-in-air-fares-next-year/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:51:46 +0000Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary predicted a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to drive up oil prices, forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers.

Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, O’Leary said on Tuesday during a press conference in Brussels. As a result, airline margins will get squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said.

“You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months,” O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.”

The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic jump in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets.

O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry.

Ryanair doesn’t expect big delivery delays on Boeing software issue

“We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said.

Ryanair dropped as much as 2.2 per cent in morning trading in Dublin, bringing the decline to about 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018.

O’Leary used his expletive-laden press conference to dish out against regulation in markets like France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He reiterated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment.

Air Baltic Corp and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over British carrier EasyJet.

Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability.

O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected through April. – Bloomberg

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445624/">
   <title>Missbrauchsprozess gegen Paal begonnen</title>
   <description>Seit Donnerstagvormittag müssen sich der Kabarettist Günther „Gunkl“ Paal und zwei Frauen, Mutter und Tochter, vor dem Landesgericht für Strafsachen Wien verantworten. Paal wird sexueller Missbrauch eines Kindes vorgeworfen, er ist geständig. Den beiden Frauen wird schwere Erpressung angelastet. Sie sollen Paal mit der Veröffentlichung von Fotos gedroht und ihn um insgesamt 189.000 Euro gebracht haben.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445731/">
   <title>Schuldzuweisungen als Wahlkampfmotor</title>
   <description>Die teils gewalttätigen Proteste in Frankreich sind wenige Monate vor der kommenden Wahl längst zum vorherrschenden Wahlkampfthema geworden. Allerorten gibt es Schuldzuweisungen. Die Regierung sieht die Verantwortung bei der Linken, die Rechten orten sie bei Migrantinnen und Migranten. Von der Spaltung, dem Schock über Eskalation und Polizeigewalt und vom Unmut der Menschen profitieren links wie rechts die Ränder.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445785/">
   <title>Meta zu 25 Mrd. Dollar Strafe verurteilt</title>
   <description>Gut acht Jahre nach dem Cambridge-Analytica-Skandal um den Missbrauch von Facebook-Nutzerdaten ist der Mutterkonzern Meta zu einem Milliardenbußgeld verurteilt worden. Ein Richter im Bundesstaat New Mexico legte die Strafe für Meta am Mittwoch auf  25 Mrd. Dollar (gut 22 Mrd. Euro) fest, wie der Sender CNBC und andere Medien berichteten. Der Konzern will das Urteil den Berichten zufolge anfechten.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445740/">
   <title>Stocker zu Kontakten mit Pilnacek befragt</title>
   <description>Im parlamentarischen U-Ausschuss zur Causa Christian Pilnacek ist am Mittwoch Bundeskanzler Christian Stocker (ÖVP) befragt worden. Im Fokus standen Kontakte mit dem später verstorbenen Ex-Justizsektionschef während der Zeit Stockers als ÖVP-Generalsekretär. Vorgelegt wurden Passagen aus dem Auswertungsbericht der Wirtschafts- und Korruptionsstaatsanwaltschaft (WKStA) zu Pilnaceks Daten, der auch direkte Korrespondenzen beinhaltet.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445771/">
   <title>Sicherheitslücken bedrohen Websites</title>
   <description>Zwei am Mittwoch einer großen Öffentlichkeit bekanntgewordene schwere Sicherheitslücken mit großem Schadpotenzial haben weltweit für Aufregung gesorgt. Zahlreiche Institutionen schalteten vorsorglich ihre Websites ab. Betroffen ist die weit verbreitete Programmiersprache PHP. Die Entwickler kündigten bereits an, dass eine neue Version zur Behebung der Sicherheitslücken verfügbar sei. Sie appellierten an alle Nutzer und Nutzerinnen, das Update sofort durchzuführen.</description>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier.

The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence.

❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta.

Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026

The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl.

Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland.

In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed.

Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026

A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border.

After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds.

One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland.

 

Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years.

In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison.

The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty.

Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client.

The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border.

The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024

In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground.

Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal.

Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.”

In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border.

A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others

The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026

In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases.

Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus.

That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross.
