]]> Poland condemns Ukrainian region for honouring figures associated with WWII massacres of Poles https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/21/poland-condemns-ukrainian-region-for-honouring-figures-associated-with-wwii-massacres-of-poles/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 09:35:45 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105802

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland.

Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska.

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026

On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).

Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice.

The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander.

While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children.

 

Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw.

“Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska.

“Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves.

Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”.

The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

 

On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News.

Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”.

Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine.

Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.…

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026

Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”.

It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.”

However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN.

The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M.

Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz

— Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026

Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession.

However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory.

But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”.

Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018.

]]> Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/21/parliament-approves-liberalisation-of-polands-abortion-laws/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:41:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105798

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok.
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

.@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️

🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026

A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS.

Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year.

Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law.

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.

 

From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.

Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.

In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.

Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026

In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.

With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.

While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.

The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.

“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”

Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years.

The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies.

📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r.

➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa

— Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026

News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”.

The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov.

“The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions.

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian).

At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people.

The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2

It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians.

There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set.

 

This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes.

In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”.

By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide.

In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres.

The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups.

Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism

It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025

In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry.

However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.

Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”.

Rathbones posted a rise in funds under management and administration as its wealth management arm returned to net inflows.

Funds under management and adminsitration increased 7.2 per cent year on year to £121.1bn.

Its wealth management arm achieved net inflows, increasing to £24m after reporting losses of £300m the previous year. 

Further growth was restricted after the FTSE 250 firm’s voluntary pause on accepting new money from enhanced due diligence (EDD) clients.

The firm also pinned the further lack of inflows on “a cautious backdrop” in the run up to the looming Autumn Budget which has caused clients to delay allocating capital to their portfolios.

But despite the rise in wealth management, clients withdrew a total net £401m from the company during the period, after increased pressure on its asset management channel.

Its asset management arm reported outflows of £425m, reflecting “continued pressure” on active equity investment in the UK retail market. Gross outflows reached £738m.

Rathbones shares nudged up 1.2 per cent to 1,618p. The stock is down by 15 per cent since the start of the year.

FCA orders

Rathbones face another multi-million pound hit after a second Financial Conduct Authority order into the wealth manager.

Rathbone’s subsidiary, Vision Independent Financial Planning, received a Section 166 notice from the City watchdog in August, which requires the FTSE 250 firm to conduct a “Skilled Person” review into the business.

The order forces businesses to appoint independent advisers to carry out a probe into the operations of the company and is used to determine whether the regulator will take enforcement action.

The provision is estimated to cost Rathbones £2.5m. The business’ future pre-tax profit is also expected to reduce by £4m from 2027 onwards due to the decline in the number of adviser firms working with them.

Rathbones will continue to manage its £1.9bn funds under management and administration (FUMA) for clients tied to the firm.

First review

Rathbones first review from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is expected to rack up costs of up to £60m, after the watchdog uncovered compliance shortcoming earlier this year.

It forced the group to stop on boarding new enhanced due diligence (EDD) clients, but it expects to lift restrictions on EDD in the fourth quarter, and said it has made “good progress” to address the findings in the Skilled Person review.

Rathbones confirmed the regulatory programme in June continues on schedule, while targeted client reviews have also started. It said no “material client outflows were attributable to the programme”.

Chief executive, Jonathan Sorrell, also doubled down on his commitment to turn Rathbones into “the best wealth manager in the UK” despite the FCA reviews.

FTSE 100 data giant Rex has reported a jump in sales growth as demand for its AI-powered products continues to rise, defying fears that the technology could threaten its business.

The London-listed group, which owns legal research platform Lexisnexis, said on Thursday that underlying revenue rose seven per cent in the first nine months of 2026, with growth across all four divisions.

Its legal business led the gains, posting a 10 per cent rise in sales as law firms increased their use of AI-powered research tools.

Relx also maintained its full-year forecast, forecasting growth in revenue, profit and earnings per share.

The update comes after a volatile year for the £51bn group, whose shares have been caught in a wider sell-off of software and data businesses amid fears that AI could replace services they currently charge customers to use.

Earlier this year, RELX shares plunged after Anthropic unveiled new AI tools capable of automating legal work, raising concerns about the future of traditional research platforms.

The sell-off, dubbed the ‘SaaSpocalypse’, hit several London-listed software firms, including Sage, as investors questioned whether established providers could compete with increasingly sophisticated AI models.

But Relx has argued that its vast stores of specialist data give it an advantage over newer AI competitors, allowing it to build products that customers are willing to pay more for.

Thursday’s figures suggest demand remains strong, although the longer-term threat from AI rivals has yet to be tested.

AI drives growth across Relx

Relx’s risk division, which provides fraud detection, identity verification and financial crime services, reported eight per cent revenue growth.

Its scientific, technical and medical business grew six per cent, supported by demand for digital research tools and rising submissions to its academic journals.

The company said its recently-launched AI research platform, Leapspace, was seeing rapid growth in usage.

Meanwhile, its exhibitions division recorded four per cent growth, with disruption in the Middle East weighing on events.

The company expects profit growth to outpace revenue growth across its legal, risk and scientific divisions this year.

The latest update comes after Relx and rival Sage enjoyed a brief reprieve in September, when calls to slow the development of advanced AI models lifted shares in companies previously seen as vulnerable to disruption.

A new £70m fund backed by the Mayor of London and the British Business Bank has launched to help growing businesses struggling to secure finance from traditional lenders.

The Future London Growth Fund, managed by investment firm FSE Group, will offer loans of between £1m and £3m to companies across London’s 32 boroughs and the City.

The fund, launched on Thursday, aims to bridge the gap between conventional bank lending and larger venture debt deals, targeting businesses with strong growth prospects that may not yet be profitable.

It has secured cornerstone commitments from the British Business Bank, which is providing £20m, and Funding London, the Mayor’s investment arm.

The launch comes as British businesses face mounting pressure over access to capital, with founders warning that funding shortages are forcing promising companies to scale overseas.

Despite London’s status as a global financial centre, smaller businesses continue to struggle to secure growth funding.

Research from the British Business Bank found that just 71 per cent of London’s business owners reported making a profit, compared with 84 per cent nationally.

The UK’s wine sector is going through a period of chop and change. The UK is still the second largest importer of wine in the world, behind only the US (and behind Germany if based on volume rather than value, respect). But as boiling temperatures stretch grape harvests to the brink in much of Europe, the UK’s domestic growing market is ripening. As grape production becomes more rooted in our landscape, will wine consumption in turn shake up our lager-drenched culture? 

A recent study by the Wine and Spirit Trade Association (WSTA) has found that although wine consumption is slowing, there is a trend towards premiumisation. In other words, less plonk more Planque. The average Brit drinks 17.5 bottles of wine a year, which to me feels puritanically low. This summer, my GP gave me a gentle scolding over my own wine consumption (which was concerning because I was lying).

But I love wine even if I’ve never been on totally sure footing talking about it. In an attempt to rationalise what I was pounding down over lockdown, I read the excellent ‘Wine from Another Galaxy’ by the Noble Rot boys. I occasionally read wine columns, a little wonkish on the vine, and diligently take pictures of bottles I drink in restaurants for the pseudo camera roll archive. Remembering wine when you don’t really know wine and are drinking said wine is a challenge in itself. But earlier this year I decided it was time to get a proper schooling in how to talk about – or at least convince others I can talk about – wine.

Bermondsey Street is one of the most European feeling streets in London. Bustling with bars and cafes, The White Cube gallery and great restaurants like Casse Croute and José Pizarro, it’s an apt home for a wine school. The Wine and Spirit Education Trust (WSET) is the global standard for booze qualifications. It offers classes in beers, sake and spirits, but wine is its bread and butter. Sommeliers from top restaurants around the world will study here for years to get the highest qualification: a Level Four Diploma. Next time you’re at a fancy restaurant, look out for the little pin badges proudly displayed by somms who have put in PhD-level graft. 

My own ambitions were more modest, namely, a full-day course to get my Level One (the difficulty between levels rises exponentially). Arriving in the morning to the classroom felt like going back to school, only here the desks were covered in wine glasses rather than pencil shavings. My class of 20 or so was pretty mixed. A WSET spokesperson explains that one of the biggest changes the school has seen since Covid is the rise of amateur enthusiasts taking courses rather than just people in hospitality and the drinks sector more widely. In my group there was one man who loved wine and had brought his mate who had “nothing better to do” on a Friday; a couple of friends wanting to order better wine when they hit the town; one guy was plotting a coup to become head bartender; a husband wanted to catch up to his Level Three wife; and some of the younger members of the class looked like their parents may have bought them the course for Christmas. 

The day is split into two halves: theory in the morning and tasting in the afternoon (you can also do Level One across two evening classes). Our teacher, who was knowledgeable and enthusiastic, took us through the basics of wine production, grape characteristics, different styles, best practices with serving, drinking and storing. It was genuinely fun, and although never super challenging, by lunchtime we could read a wine list and know more or less what to expect from the bottle. 

During the lunch break I was so geed-up on wine learning that I went and spent a small fortune on bottles of wine from 40 Maltby Street. Sadly my words failed me when met with the incredibly cool, natural wine connoisseurs working there. 

The afternoon session is a little blurrier. Spitting was encouraged, but not enforced. It was an amazing experience to taste along with a sommelier as they throw out words that in that exact sip, makes total sense: green pepper, Haribo, stewed plums, Petits Filous yoghurt, apricot, clove, menthol cigarettes, tarte Tatin, black olives and manure. Our teacher told us that one of the best ways to develop your palate is just to smell everything you come across, which I’ve been doing – slightly deranged baby-esque – ever since. 

The Level One course was a gentle expanding of what wine can be – and how it doesn’t always need to adhere to rigid rules. At the end of the day you take an exam, which also reminded me of going back to school in a less good way with its big ticking clock and candidate numbers. Had I known it was exam conditions, I might have gone lighter in the sampling. But brimming with overconfidence I breezed through and got an email a couple of weeks later confirming I’d passed – not, however, without a few mistakes.

Not to worry, it just gives me something to aim for when I take my Level Two. 

Want to learn more about wine? Here’s a breakdown of the qualifications run by WSET:

  • At Level 1, you’ll learn the fundamentals in an approachable way, helping you explore and enjoy drinks with greater confidence.  
  • At Level 2, that confidence grows into broader knowledge and understanding. You’ll learn to compare products, understand how production influences style and quality, and develop a more structured approach to tasting and evaluation.  
  • At Level 3, learners move from understanding to explanation. They gain a deeper knowledge of production, style and quality, while developing the analytical tasting skills needed to confidently assess, describe and explain why a wine, beer or spirit tastes the way it does. 
  • For those who continue to the WSET Level 4 Diploma in Wines, the emphasis is on expert-level analysis and evaluation, preparing students for senior industry roles or advanced study.

It’s baffling that sport’s global leaders are still prevaricating over Russia as the LA28 Olympics and Paralympics draw ever nearer, says Ed Warner.

To Brentford FC’s Gtech Community Stadium last week for the second outing of The NEDwork, a gathering of chairs and non-executive directors from across Great Britain’s Olympic and Paralympic governing bodies. 

Russia’s return to the Games, and the chaotic way in which it is being handled, was the principal concern of the chairs of Britain’s OLY and PLY sports when I spoke to them. Specifically, the inconsistent approaches of the IOC, the IPC and the individual international sport federations that control their component sports.

Eleven years on from the eruption of Russia’s doping scandal and four and a half years after its invasion of Ukraine, it is baffling that the rulers of global sport are still unable to agree on a coherent response to these twin severe challenges that President Putin’s regime has posed to its moral code.

Remember the hole in the wall at the Sochi 2014 anti-doping lab? Well, this still stands as a shocking totem of the systemic doping that drove a wedge between the IOC and key affected sports, especially athletics. 

It also divided the Olympic and Paralympic movements – the IPC adopting a tougher stance towards Russian participation at Rio 2016 and jeopardising its financial and operational dependence on the IOC as a result.

Initial responses to the war in Ukraine were largely uniform, matching the watching world’s condemnation of Putin’s assault. In time, though, the outright ban on Russian athletes has steadily eroded. 

That may be the result of simple fatigue, the nagging caution of legal advisors, the softer stance of Russia’s natural allies or realpolitik from those anxious to court favour with President Trump ahead of the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Whatever the mix of forces, sport’s attitude to Russian participation in international events ranges widely. Athletics still won’t allow it (having for a while, pre-war, softened its position to allow heavily-tested athletes to compete as “neutrals”); a string of sports permit selected Russian neutrals without their national flag or anthem; the IPC has swung from hardline to soft and beat the IOC to full restoration of rights; and the IOC has shifted in the same direction but is hiding behind the line that it is up to individual sports to decide.

With all due respect to the Paralympics – and I write as chair of GB Wheelchair Rugby, albeit in a personal capacity here – it is the IOC’s morphing position that has caused such angst, not just in Britain but much more widely. 

The organisation’s presidential baton passed from Thomas Bach to Kirsty Coventry in 2025. Both are arch pragmatists keen at all times to court approbation across the globe, and conscious that success in IOC elections rests on garnering votes from the many smaller nations rather than the wealthy few.

Map a one-member, one-vote organisational democracy against Russia’s spheres of influence and it becomes easy to understand why Western European arguments in favour of sporting sanctions carry less sway than their proponents might hope or expect. The old adage about the value of seeing things from your opponent’s perspective holds true. Little wonder many administrators end up feeling impotent.

It is hard to know whether individual sports are providing leadership to the IOC on the Russia question, or vice versa. What we do know is that judo, taekwondo, aquatics and fencing, for example, now allow the full flummery of national kit, flags and anthem as well as Russian athletes themselves. Still no place for senior Russian football teams, though, given that Fifa’s ban remains.

“We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”

Kuwait’s Husain Al-Musallam, President of World Aquatics, April 2026

Much of the agonising by Britain‘s governing bodies over Russia stems from their duties to the athletes who compete for Team GB and ParalympicsGB. In part, this has an eye on the make-up of the competition and GB medal prospects; but more significantly this reflects the realisation that athletes are the people who will be in the media spotlight at Games time. Their soundbites will be the ones that reverberate. Any decision to shake hands or share a podium would constitute a propaganda photo op for the Russian regime.

If you doubt how tricky this might be, just consider the moral knot that Irish football has tied itself up in recently. Two men’s Nations League matches have taken place between the Republic of Ireland and Israel in neutral venues, the Irish team coming under intense pressure at home to take a stance against Israeli actions in Gaza. 

The players found themselves in an invidious position when presumably all they want to do is pursue their sporting ambitions. Whether their football association and Uefa did right by them is up for debate, your own stance likely depending on your view of the Gaza conflict.

Multiply this situation – by no means black and white – by the number of athletes who might compete against Russians and Belarusians at LA28 and you can see that the opportunity for noise, uncertainty and grandstanding is enormous. A media godsend, although possibly the sheer quantity of stories will dull their edge as the twin Games progress.

It is by no means clear that Donald Trump would want to welcome Russian athletes to LA28 with full team accoutrements, but his current rhetoric about the war in Ukraine might suggest that Russia’s participation would carry a symbolism consistent with his desire to force conflict resolution.

”I am optimistic about further progress that would establish a reliable mechanism for fuller participation by Russian athletes at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.”

US President Trump’s special envoy, Paolo Zampolli, interviewed by TASS last week. The next day he announced he’d left his post

With the Games still the best part of two years away, you might assume there is plenty of time for this issue to be resolved, but that is to ignore qualification processes that will begin in earnest next year. 

The IOC’s softer stance was announced too close to this year’s Winter Olympics to make much difference to the number of Russian and Belarusian athletes who took part. With the much greater profile and scale of a Summer Games, those advocating inclusion will be aware they need to push hard now if they are to secure a near full-strength Russian presence in LA.

Whatever the outcome, there will be athletes put on the spot and asked to take a stance either way, Ukrainians included. Each deserves leaders prepared to provide moral cover, not so that they can shelve their own consciences, but because true responsibility should lie with those in charge of global sport who have abdicated that responsibility so abjectly to date.

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

This has led to the overhaul of tenant protections, including abolishing no-fault evictions, replacing fixed-term contracts with rolling periodic tenancies, and effectively ending rent increases. However, some economists have questioned the Act’s effectiveness and raised concerns that the reforms would actually harm renters in the long run.

    Valentin Boboc, senior economist at the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA), told City AM: “Landlords are more likely to quit when letting becomes less profitable and more uncertain.     However, another concern is the pressure these changes will put on the country’s legal system.

    The housing minister, Matthew Pennycook MP, posted on social media on Tuesday that the Labour government’s Renters’ Rights Act “empowers private renters to challenge unreasonable rent increases”, adding that Brits can now refer the matter to the First-Tier Tribunal (FTT). He shared a link to a recent legal judgment in his post on X in which someone challenged their landlord in court over a rent increase, only to have the rent reduced – by more than the proposed increase.

    On top of warning against bringing the courts into it, Silvia Andreoletti, head of communications at the Adam Smith Institute, told City AM, “setting rents through Tribunals rather than the free market is a policy bound to fail.”

    Surge in Tribunal cases

    The major problem with the government’s bold vision is that it pushes people toward Tribunals, which are already backlogged or at risk of becoming backlogged because of the increased workload as a result of these new reforms.

    Rent cases go to the First-tier Tribunal, Property Chambers, which has reportedly already seen a surge in cases. As the Act came into force in May, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said the first complete three-month period (quarter) in which the new rules were fully in effect across all cases was July to September, and those figures will be published in December.

    Andreoletti added that as “almost three-quarters of Tribunals find in favour of the tenant”, she added, “any rational tenant would jump at the opportunity to take any [rent] increase to Tribunal.”

    The government was questioned on this matter earlier this year. Sarah Sackman MP reassured Parliament that while the MoJ expects more cases due to housing reforms, the department is managing it through digital upgrades and by centralising staff for Tribunals.

    As of April 2026, the MoJ has 112 judges sitting in the First-Tier Tribunal (Property Chamber).

    A government spokesperson told City AM: “Our Renters’ Rights Act empowers tenants to challenge unreasonable rent increases, with a recent Manchester case seeing a tribunal determine that the market rate was £200 below the landlord’s proposed level. 

    “We are supporting all courts and tribunals to cope with potential additional pressure by maximising sitting days and continuing to invest in the annual recruitment of up to 1,000 judges and tribunal members across all jurisdictions.”

    But it seems to be the solution for all its major overhauls. The government’s major change to employment rights law is now putting severe pressure on the Employment Tribunal, which was already suffering from a backlog formed during the pandemic.

    The latest figures show that the Employment Tribunal backlog has hit record highs, with around 70,000 to 77,594 open single claims and over 467,000 total open cases. Lawyers have said some case listings in parts of London and the South East Tribunals stretch into 2028, 2029, and even 2030.

    Employment lawyers have been vocal about how strained the Tribunal is, and predictions suggest the pressure will worsen as Employment Rights Act rights, which are spaced out over the next couple of years, all come into force.

    Although the government has ruled out raising Capital Gains Tax in the upcoming budget, Labour’s broader tax and spending policies remain economically damaging, uncompetitive, and fundamentally misguided, says Daniel Herring

    The government needs to find money for the upcoming Budget. Having ruled out the least damaging and broadest-based tax rises, Labour needs to resort to little taxes here and there to find money. Raising capital gains tax (CGT), even aligning it with income tax, was seen as a way that raised revenue while avoiding hurting working people. There’s support for this Cabinet:  Wes Streeting called CGT a “wealth tax that works”. Louise Haigh is another prominent advocate. It is superficially appealing: why should different forms of income be treated differently?

    However, CGT is a damaging tax and raising it is likely to be counterproductive. Thankfully the government has ruled out raising capital gains tax in the upcoming budget. 

    CGT is paid by a small number of people: 32,000 taxpayers account for 80 per cent of CGT revenue, and 5,000 account for half. Furthermore, people choose when to sell their assets. If they choose to hold an asset that would be better used by someone else in the economy (or sell prematurely ahead of a rise), that asset could be used less productively than if it had been owned by someone else. There is evidence of people moving the sale of assets to avoid paying CGT. 

    For these reasons, raising CGT could even lose money while being economically damaging. HMRC estimates that raising the higher rate of CGT by 10 points could lower revenue by £3.6bn after three years.

    It also makes the UK uncompetitive. On Monday the Tax Foundation published the International Tax Competitiveness Index, which looks at how pro-growth tax systems are in the OECD. The UK comes 30th out of 38. Currently our highest CGT rate is 24 per cent, which is roughly in the middle of OECD countries. But in analysis I’ve done at the Centre for Policy Studies, raising it to 45 per cent would make the UK’s rate the highest in the world, and would make the lower UK’s overall tax competitiveness rank to 32nd. 

    The most respectable argument is that we should align CGT with income tax while introducing a generous allowance that allows for inflation (some call for an allowance even higher than inflation, called the normal rate of return, but leave that to one side). 

    Taxing entrepreneurship

    There are good arguments to be made for this, but I still have concerns. In practice what this would mean is that most people paying CGT on very modest nominal gains today would pay no CGT, while a much smaller group who have extraordinary gains would have to pay more. This group would include our most innovative entrepreneurs – you want to be very careful about increasing taxes on this group. 

    But back to Labour. John Healey is walking a tightrope between markets and backbenchers. His backbenchers largely want to see increased spending, while business and markets want to see spending constraint and pro-growth reforms. In this case, he’s leaned towards listening to the likes of Jim O’Neill, who has said that raising CGT would send “the wrong message to business”. 

    Does this decision make John Healey a pro-growth Chancellor? I don’t think so. Ultimately, if growth was this government’s number one priority it would be finding ways to reduce taxes on business by cutting spending. There are other damaging taxes he will introduce, including a tax on banks. These are likely to raise little revenue and raise the cost of capital. These taxes come on top of already damaging tax rises made by Rachel Reeves, most notably the increase in employer national insurance. 

    Besides not really prioritising growth, all of this points to another fundamental misunderstanding within Labour. All countries that have higher spending governments raise most of their revenue through higher taxes on ordinary workers. You can either have a high spending state with high taxes on ordinary workers. Or you can have a low spending state with low taxes on ordinary people. Labour needs to choose which kind of state it wants. You cannot fund a high spending state while trying to squeeze only the rich. There aren’t enough of them and they’ll all leave. 

    Daniel Herring is head of economic and fiscal policy at the Centre for Policy Studies

    It’s pure delusion to conclude that rejoining the European Union would cure our financial woes and the public knows it, says Dr Michael Turner

    Andy Burnham wants to reopen Pandora’s box. After solemnly promising before the Makerfield by-election that Brexit was settled, the Prime Minister now concludes that all options are on the table as part of a rethink of Britain’s relationship with the bloc. He joins a chorus of Westminster sentimentalists who insist Britain’s current economic stagnation is a purely self-inflicted wound from Brexit in 2016, and that only rejoining can resolve it. It’s a seductive narrative that suits a government with many problems, but few ideas. But it fundamentally misdiagnoses the issue.

    Our latest City AM / Freshwater Strategy Poll shows the public’s lacklustre mood: two-thirds (66 per cent) of UK voters believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, while a similar number (65 per cent) are not confident in the government’s plan to achieve economic growth. Meanwhile, half (50 per cent) expect the national economy to worsen over the next 12 months, and half believe that raising taxes in the forthcoming budget would demonstrate the government’s economic failure rather than prudence. 

    It’s pure delusion to conclude that rejoining the European Union would cure our financial woes.

    Britain’s economic stagnation has little to do with leaving the Single Market. More important is the decade-long relay race of anti-business, high-tax, statist management from several governments, blue and red. From Theresa May and Boris Johnson to Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer, and now Andy Burnham, we have seen a series of leaders who don’t understand what actually generates wealth and prosperity.

    A return to the debate over Europe won’t fix our domestic fiscal ineptitude, but will distract us from addressing it and inevitably tear the country apart once again.

    We spent half the last decade watching British politicians squabble over whether to deliver on the original democratic mandate, and the other half struggling to deal with Covid. Brits have no appetite for a second decade of constitutional civil war. They want cheaper energy bills, more homes, more runways, an economy where people can afford a holiday, a new car, and to feel more secure in their job.

    Anyone who works on deals for a living can see that Brussels is not in the business of charitable negotiation. Over the past decade, the EU’s treatment of the UK has focused on showing its remaining members that while membership can be costly, leaving the bloc is much more painful.

    Most glaringly, the EU’s cynical use of Northern Ireland as a permanent geopolitical lever has revealed an institution that is legalistic (when it suits them), punitive, and ideologically worlds apart from Britain’s more market-led financial approach, whatever is left of it.

    Our City AM / Freshwater Strategy Poll asked a series of questions about what might make people interested in rejoining the EU. While the toplines may excite the rejoin crowd, there is an inconvenient catch. 

    On face value there is majority support for rejoining (50 per cent). And this rises further if rejoining means frictionless trade and the ability for Brits to live, work, study, and retire anywhere in the EU (62 per cent).

    Mirage

    But the toplines are a mirage. 

    Of course it would be nice if we did have to queue at customs, if we could have more choice to live and study abroad. It would be ideal if British businesses weren’t held up by bureaucracy when trying to trade with businesses on the continent. 

    But as with any membership organisation, just because there are perks, doesn’t mean people sign up at any cost.

    The trouble for the re-joiners is that public support shifts dramatically once they learn about Brussels’ non-negotiables.

    Any referendum on rejoining will not be a vote on abstract goodwill; it will be a vote on how many more billions UK taxpayers will have to pay, whether to adopt the Euro, how many more politicians to add to the payroll, whether to relinquish fiscal control, and whether to accept regulatory alignment without a veto

    If rejoining means paying more than ever into the EU budget, just 30 per cent would support the move, while 37 per cent oppose. Forcing them to confront joining the Eurozone reduces support to just one-quarter (26 per cent) and a majority of voters oppose (50 per cent).

    Any opposition campaign worth its salt will simply put those non-negotiables on repeat, and re-join will be dead before you can paint £350m on the side of a red bus.

    Our problem isn’t that we are outside the EU; it’s that our political class has bought into Johnson-style ‘have-it-all’ cakeism and refuses to make difficult short-term political choices for sustained economic growth. It’s time to stop chasing continental mirages and start fixing Britain’s business.

    Dr Michael Turner is co-founder and Director at Freshwater Strategy

    Flying cars have been a dream for 100 years, but culture war cynicism is preventing us from getting excited about Elon Musk’s Roadster, writes Anna Moloney

    In Illustrated World, 1917, beneath a gleaming image of a red car with eagle-like wings, an article in the American monthly science magazine predicted: “The aeroautocraft of the future will roll on the road, cleave through the water, fly through the air. Its owner will start from his garage or hangar, travel streets or roads at will, cross streams or lakes that lie in his path, rise in the air and fly over a hill, a valley, or woods, to another road, all at his pleasure. This is not the prediction of a dreamer, but the logical development of present day tendencies.”

    A beaming illustration of technological optimism, published more than a hundred years ago.

    Flying cars have long been the symbol of the future – representing not just technical progress, but the ultimate dream of American freedom. To not just go west, but to fly upwards.

    We may then have reasonably expected that Elon Musk’s unveiling last week of the Roadster, Tesla’s flying car prototype – which uses SpaceX thrusters to propel itself into the air, and even perform a couple of flips – to have been cause for genuine excitement. A flying car! What science fiction fantasists have been dreaming up for more than a century! Instead, beyond Musk’s own faithful base of tech bros and fanboys, the reception, it is fair to say, was largely muted and, where it has been covered, made up overwhelmingly of straight-faced reports urging painfully serious questions: Is the Roadster road safe? Does anyone actually want a flying car? Et cetera. Et cetera.

    Excuse my yawning, but can we all stop being such bores. (No, of course it’s not road safe! Yes, people do want flying cars!) For me, the far more pressing concern is where has all the wonder gone, and can we get it back please?

    This is a far more insidious iteration of the “permanent underclass” fear that drives many Silicon Valley founders and workers. That fear was centred on capitalism’s tendency to create monopolies.

No individual human, however brilliant, can outcompete a corporation or hyper- wealthy individual able to deploy vast amounts of capital into compute.     In a world where almost everyone is born outside the tiny group of perhaps 5,000 People who control the bulk of this wealth and compute, intelligence, talent and hard work cease to offer a meaningful route to a better life. Almost nobody can change their station, because no individual can compete with “intelligence” deployed at industrial scale. It does not solve the fundamental equation that more capital buys more compute, and therefore more “intelligence”, but it is a start.

    Fundamentally, people must be able to make decisions about their own futures rather than having them dictated by a small group of bro-ligarchs.

After a three-year battle, the Scottish court quashed the original consent, handing the activists a major victory and forcing its operators to resubmit their environmental assessments.

    Why was Jackdaw approved?

    Despite the environmental zealotry of her predecessor, now-foreign secretary Ed Miliband, Fahnbulleh’s approval is not surprising. Before he had even won a seat in parliament, her boss was promising to take a more “pragmatic approach” to Britain’s North Sea energy assets. Since then, be it at last month’s Labour party conference or during several media appearances, “pragmatism” has been the line that he and Fahnbulleh have repeated ad nauseam since.

    It is a notably – and deliberately – vague commitment. But whatever one’s interpretation, it was always likely to spell good news for Jackdaw. Gas – and Jackdaw consists entirely of natural gas – will be part of the UK’s energy mix for decades no matter how successful our energy transition. If we have to rely on gas, simple logic dictates, why not reap the economic and environmental benefits of doing so domestically rather than shipping it from abroad?

    The mental veil we drape over our troubling physiology is perhaps at its thinnest when we are making and rearing children: growing them, squeezing them out, suckling them. Ew.     The majority of the film charts Saga’s slow, excruciating psychological breakdown, punctuated by moments of gratuitous body horror. As she births their (incredibly hairy) child, Jon’s face is splattered by a geyser of blood; Saga inspects the viscous red material that gathers in her knickers after the traumatic birth; the baby gnaws her nipples until they flow with crimson.     British energy unicorn Fuse is moving into AI infrastructure, betting that its control over electricity supply will allow it to build data centres faster than rivals struggling with lengthy grid delays.

    The London-based company, founded by former Revolut executives Alan Chang and Charles Orr, has launched Fuse Compute, offering businesses access to Nvidia chips hosted in UK data centres powered by Fuse.

    Its first 128 Nvidia B300 GPUs are expected to come online in December, rising to 1,024 by the second quarter of 2027. The company then plans to add 22 megawatts (MW) of data centre power capacity in late 2027, with a further 116MW planned from 2028.

    “Energy costs are only five per cent of GPU rental revenues, so energy costs are not a significant consideration when pricing GPU rentals”, Chang told City AM. “The key advantage Fuse possesses is energy availability, which means much faster speed to stand up data centres, and this will allow our compute customers to scale up much faster”.

    His comments challenge the idea that cheaper renewable energy alone could give Fuse a pricing advantage in the increasingly competitive market for AI computing power.

    The move marks a significant departure for the $5bn (£3.7bn) energy business, which launched in 2022 and now supplies electricity to 470,000 British households.

    It comes as the government’s ambitions to make Britain a global AI powerhouse face mounting pressure from electricity shortages and delays connecting data centres to the grid.

    Earlier this week, Microsoft pulled out of a planned £2bn AI data centre project in Essex after developer Nscale was told securing sufficient grid power could be delayed until the 2030s.

    The setback has renewed questions over Britain’s ability to deliver the infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions.

    “Fuse has been building energy infrastructure since before the AI wave”, Chang added. “We have a deep understanding of energy infrastructure that many other data centre developers do not possess”.

    Can Fuse deliver?

    Fuse has 142MW of data centre connections in its pipeline across 15 projects, alongside more than 1GW of planned power generation.

    It says its latest solar development was built around 30 per cent below the industry average cost, giving it an advantage over competitors reliant on third-party energy suppliers.

    But those savings will not necessarily translate into cheaper AI computing. Chang said Fuse would price its GPUs competitively, rather than promising to undercut established providers.

    Its December launch will comprise just 128 Nvidia B300 GPUs, while the far larger developments planned for 2027 and 2028 have yet to come online. The company has not disclosed pricing and contracts will be negotiated individually.

    Fuse is also pitching itself as a British alternative to overseas cloud providers, offering domestic AI companies greater control over where their data is processed.

    “Compute is critical national infrastructure,” Chang said. “British AI companies can keep sensitive data and models fully under UK jurisdiction”.

    He added that overseas AI companies could also use Fuse’s UK facilities to serve British customers with lower latency”.

    The company expects its near-term data centre projects to represent £1bn of UK infrastructure investment and support 250 construction and operational jobs.

    The expansion follows rapid growth in its energy business, which reached group-level profitability earlier this year.

    Speaking to City AM in June, Chang blamed Britain’s planning system for holding back infrastructure investment.

    “There is more money chasing infrastructure projects than there are infrastructure projects”, he said, calling it a “self-imposed bottleneck for growth”.

    The government’s Compute Roadmap estimates Britain will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030.

    All of these new luxury hotels opening up are making us believe that “discretion” is the key to luxury, and if that is the case, surely The Old Doctor Butler’s Head is the most opulent venue in London. Tucked down a pedestrian alley in the heart of the Square Mile, you only know it when you know it, and the excitement of first discovery is such that you’ll want to take that turning again and again with different friends, and go “look what’s here!”

    Outside on that alleyway, City workers gather so tightly around upturned beer barrels that people trying to pass from one end to the other literally give up and come in for a pint. Inside, it’s Dickensian cosy or Dickensian rambunctious, depending on whether you’re near the bar or sitting in the tiered seating at the back. Towards the back of the ground floor, old illustrated maps of London and chalked up blackboards with daily food menus are lit by vintage brass wall lamps.

    Inside the Old Doctor Butler’s Head

    Get away from the chattering bankers by booking a table to dine upstairs. There, in the more serene carpeted room, tables offer views out to the drinking masses, as well as practically into the windows of the handsome Tudor reconstruction building on the other side of the alleyway. Up here, worn tomes sit atop an original fireplace framed by cofferred wooden walls, and framed City of London coat of arms certificates hang on the walls.

    The pub originally opened in 1610, although the original structure was destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666. The current building was built shortly after the blaze and is the last pub named in homage to Dr William Butler, a court physician to King James I whose “medicinal purging ale” was sold at his eponymous taverns.

    Now operated by the fairly small pub group Shepherd Neame, who operate around 300 pubs and hotels throughout the South East, the menu offers promises honest pub food. When I dined one Friday lunchtime, we had our pick of the upstairs tables, which felt good, given the scrum downstairs probably didn’t even realise upstairs dining was an option.

    My friend and I started with a generous sausage roll which we ripped into two, as well as some very juicy battered prawns. For mains, I had the pie of the day, with chicken, which was handmade with great, well-balanced pastry; just the right amount of butter to be indulgent but also firm enough to hold its innards without collapsing. My guest enjoyed a lighter but still indulgent chicken kiev sandwich.

    ‘People love the pub as it is’

    The pub has recently taken on a new manager, Rebecca Whittome, who came over from the Samuel Pepys pub on the Thames. They’ll potentially get a refurbishment budget next year to straighten out some of the wooden floorboards and extend the downstairs bar, but Whittome insists any amplifications will take a less-is-more approach. “People love it as it is,” she says. “We won’t stray too far from the feel of this place.” Though, a few corners could do with more lighting, says Whittome, who also has ambitions to drive an increase in corporate and events bookings to their first and second floor rooms, the highest of which has space for 70 and the middle floor with space for 30. We go right to the top and it’s another handsome room: given their history and atmosphere, it’s a shame these spots aren’t booked out every night of the week.

    Not that there’s any issue with pint pouring downstairs. “People come here for the vibe,” says Whittome succintly. I won’t name them, for fear of being barred from Dr Butler’s Head, but there really are only a handful of other City watering hotels that can compete with the atmosphere drummed up here, by that eccentric old Doctor Butler.

    One of the Square Mile sights you might have missed over the years is the former brewery a stone’s throw from the Barbican. The grand old building is now owned by the Montcalm Collection, the London hotel firm that specialises in period conversions. Their Mayfair property repurposes a row of Georgian townhouses, and their Finsbury Square property is within the former Royal Mail headquarters.

    As for the city branch, this Montcalm property extends beyond the hotel to The Chiswell Street Dining Rooms and The Jugged Hare pub over the road. Also formerly parts of the brewery, they have transformed into luxury food joints, 40 years since the last beer was brewed on the site.

    The pub has taxidermy hares as per its namesake, as well as a litany of other wild animals hanging rather unceremoniously from its walls, and a traditional pub atmosphere with very good food. The Chiswell Street Dining Rooms, however, is more traditional and refined, again with a best of British approach. 

    Inside the Montcalm Brewery

    Anyway, back to the hotel, and rooms fuse period historical charm with modern functionality. Bedrooms are spacious, many with four-poster beds, and classic sash windows, with views out onto the never-changing Georgian streets and the Barbican beyond.

    There’s also an on-site Montcalm Brewery fitness suite.

    As for the benefits of Montcalm, early check-in and late check-out are offered as standard if they are available, as are complimentary room upgrades.

    And you’re a two minute amble away from a leading cultural institution, with all of its exhibitions, theatre shows, live gigs, cinema, restaurants and events programming.
