Choose the commutation method according to motion quality

Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior.

Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations.

Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning.

Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components.

The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM).

In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM.

FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications.

FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error.

Select the feedback architecture

Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems.

Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information.

Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence.

Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important.

The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position.

That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase.

Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy.

Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate.

Match the controller to the robotic arm

A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback.

A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control.

This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task.

An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller.

The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier.

The Robot Report‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components.

For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function.

Match the controller to the mobile robot

BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment.

A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide.

Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods of sustained power.

Battery behavior also changes the controller decision. Voltage sag under acceleration reduces the available electrical headroom, while regenerative braking can raise DC bus voltage. A controller designed around a nominal battery voltage therefore needs to be evaluated over the complete battery operating range rather than at one nominal value.

Thermal design is another difference. A drive enclosed inside a wheel or compact chassis may have limited airflow. The inverter, motor windings, bearings, connectors, and mechanical structure all become part of the heat path.

Harmonic Drive‘s servo-grade propulsion drive trains for AMRs illustrate this system-level relationship. Their characteristics include smooth travel, backdrivability, torque density, stiffness, and radial load support. The lesson is not that one transmission is appropriate for every AMR, but that propulsion control cannot be separated from the drivetrain.

Mobile manipulators make the distinction even more obvious. Desmasa’s MCR+ combined a robot arm and an AMR that shared one power and control architecture. The drive requirements of the base remained different from those of the arm, even though both ultimately contained electric actuators.

Evaluate current sensing and thermal behavior

Controller current ratings require careful interpretation. A datasheet may list continuous phase current, continuous bus current, peak phase current, peak current duration, RMS current, or a configurable current limit. These numbers are not interchangeable.

The motor’s thermal limit, inverter semiconductor limit, connector rating, cable rating, and battery capability can all be lower than a headline peak current specification. A controller advertised with a large peak current is therefore not automatically suitable for a motor that requires that current continuously.

BLDC.com provides a useful commercial example of the specification categories engineers encounter in controller selection. Its current controller catalog lists different input voltage ranges and current ratings across several controller families, while individual products describe interfaces and protection features.

Those specifications illustrate why engineers should compare voltage range, current definition, duration, feedback compatibility, and protection functions rather than simply comparing wattage.

The heat path must also be considered. Motor winding losses have to leave the motor through its structure and mounting arrangement. Power stage losses must leave the inverter through its enclosure, thermal interface, heat sink, airflow, or mounting structure. Thermal testing under the actual duty cycle is more informative than relying only on a short unloaded bench test.

Consider the communications and software layers

The motor controller is normally responsible for the fastest control loops. A robot controller does not need to calculate every PWM transition. Instead, the drive can execute current regulation and commutation locally while receiving higher level torque, velocity, or position commands.

Before selecting a drive, engineers should check CAN or CANopen support, EtherCAT support, RS 485 or UART, analog and PWM inputs, encoder interfaces, feedback update rates, command latency, fault reporting, firmware update procedures, parameter storage, multi axis synchronization, ROS 2 or ros2_control integration, and CiA 402 support where applicable.

CANopen’s CiA 402 profile standardizes functional behavior for servo drives and other motion control devices, including operating states and command/status structures. That can simplify interoperability when the selected hardware actually implements the required profile.

EtherCAT becomes attractive when synchronized multi axis motion and deterministic timing are central requirements. Its distributed clock architecture allows participating devices to synchronize their local timing.

ROS 2 integration is a separate consideration from the physical bus. Ros2_control represents robot hardware through command and state interfaces and provides a framework for connecting controllers to physical actuators. The controller manager also emphasizes deterministic control loop execution, showing why communication availability alone does not guarantee real time behavior.

Treat safety as an architecture, not a checkbox

A motor controller should be evaluated for overcurrent, short circuit, overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, overspeed, encoder failure, Hall failure, phase loss, stall detection, brake control, communications loss, regenerative voltage rise, unintended restart, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque off where applicable.

These functions are not automatically equivalent to a complete safety architecture. Safety requirements depend on the robot category, risk assessment, operating environment, and system design.

For industrial robots, ISO 10218 1:2025 specifies safety requirements for industrial robots. ISO 13849 1:2023 addresses the design of safety related parts of control systems, including software. IEC 61800 5 2 addresses functional safety considerations for safety related adjustable speed power drive systems.

The important engineering distinction is that a controller having an overcurrent shutdown or temperature sensor does not, by itself, establish a certified safety function. The safety function has to be designed, validated, and integrated according to the applicable requirements.

A practical selection workflow

A useful motor controller selection process can be reduced to ten engineering steps.

  • Step 1: Define the complete load and motion profile, including acceleration, deceleration, payload, terrain, gravity, and duty cycle.
  • Step 2: Calculate continuous and peak torque at the motor shaft and, where applicable, at the joint or wheel.
  • Step 3: Establish the required speed, acceleration, operating range, and regenerative braking conditions.
  • Step 4: Define the control objective: speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction.
  • Step 5: Select feedback according to the actual control objective and mechanical transmission.
  • Step 6: Select six step, sinusoidal, or FOC control based on motion quality, speed range, torque requirements, and implementation constraints.
  • Step 7: Check voltage, continuous and peak current, regeneration, thermal margins, and battery behavior.
  • Step 8: Select the communication and software interfaces needed by the robot architecture.
  • Step 9: Define safety behavior, fault response, braking, communication loss behavior, and restart conditions.
  • Step 10: Validate the complete motor, drive, gearbox, sensor, brake, and robot controller as one system.

BLDC motor control selection decision table

Application requirement Preferred control direction Main reason Important limitation
Simple wheel speed control Sensored six step or simple closed loop control Low implementation complexity Coarser torque and position behavior
High-efficiency mobile traction FOC with appropriate feedback Good torque and speed regulation across a wide operating range Higher software and tuning complexity
Low-speed robotic joint motion Encoder based FOC Smooth torque production and precise rotor angle information Transmission and tuning still limit performance
High precision joint positioning Servo drive with encoder feedback, potentially output feedback Position loop can account for joint behavior More sensors, wiring, and integration effort
Torque controlled collaborative joint FOC servo architecture with suitable torque feedback or estimation Fast current/torque response Safety and torque accuracy require system validation
Sensorless high speed drive Sensorless commutation or sensorless FOC Eliminates position sensors and wiring Startup and very low speed behavior require careful design
Multi axis synchronized arm Networked servo drives, often with deterministic Ethernet Coordinated timing and distributed control Network and drive configuration become part of commissioning
Harsh outdoor mobile robot Closed loop drive with feedback selected for the environment Better speed control, diagnostics, and traction management Environmental sealing and thermal design remain system level issues

Commissioning and validation

A controller should not move directly from a wiring diagram to production operation. First, verify phase order and encoder direction. Confirm Hall or encoder alignment and current sense polarity. Run the motor unloaded at reduced voltage where the hardware permits it, then compare commanded and measured speed.

Next, check position error and current behavior. Apply a controlled mechanical load and measure phase current and bus current. Monitor motor and inverter temperatures during acceleration, steady operation, and repeated cycles.

Regenerative braking deserves a dedicated test. Measure the DC bus during controlled deceleration and confirm that the battery, braking circuit, and controller remain within their operating limits.

Communication loss testing should verify what the drive actually does when commands stop arriving. Sensor disconnection tests should confirm fault detection and the resulting state. Overcurrent, thermal protection, emergency stop, and brake behavior should also be tested under controlled conditions.

Finally, repeat the important tests after thermal soak. A drive that behaves correctly for several minutes at room temperature may behave differently after the motor and inverter reach their operating temperatures.

For a robotic arm, these tests should be performed with the gearbox and representative mechanism installed. For a mobile robot, they should include the actual wheel, vehicle mass, battery, terrain, and representative duty cycle. A bench test of an unloaded motor validates only part of the system.

Engineer’s checklist

  1. What are the continuous and peak torque requirements?
  2. What is the required speed and acceleration range?
  3. Is the objective speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction control?
  4. Is Hall feedback sufficient, or is encoder feedback required?
  5. Is motor side feedback sufficient for the mechanical transmission?
  6. Does six step control provide adequate motion quality, or is FOC justified?
  7. Are voltage, current, regeneration, and thermal margins adequate?
  8. Does the communications interface meet latency and synchronization requirements?
  9. What happens during sensor failure, communication loss, braking, and emergency stop?
  10. Has the complete actuator been tested under the actual mechanical duty cycle?

Pulling together criteria to pick the right motor

The correct BLDC motor control architecture is determined by the control variable, mechanical transmission, feedback quality, duty cycle, thermal limits, energy system, safety architecture, and software integration.

For a simple mobile drive, a sensored six-step controller may provide an adequate combination of cost, robustness, and speed regulation. A demanding robotic joint may instead require encoder based FOC, nested torque, velocity, and position loops, and possibly output side feedback.

An outdoor mobile platform may need closed loop traction control, careful regenerative energy management, environmental protection, and thermal capacity that would be unnecessary on a small indoor robot.

The key decision is therefore not simply which BLDC motor controller has the right voltage or wattage rating. The useful question is whether the complete motor, inverter, feedback system, transmission, power source, communications layer, and safety architecture can produce the required behavior throughout the robot’s actual operating envelope.

The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI.

AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world.

Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report. Success will depend on more than model performance. It will require advances across sensing, simulation, computing, connectivity, and control.

A machine that reads vibration, temperature, current, and motor behavior; recognizes the signature of bearing wear; and adjusts before failure occurs is doing something closer to judgment.

That distinction helps explain why physical AI has become one of the most closely watched areas in technology for manufacturing. These systems do more than analyze information. They interact with the world around them, adapting to changing conditions and responding to situations that cannot be fully predicted in advance.

The next phase of physical and embodied AI is not simply about producing better answers. It is about predicting and producing useful actions in the presence of imperfect information, said ADI. To read the full whitepaper, click here: The Race to Make AI Physical.

The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid, shown here, is an example of a robot ready for AI.

For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work.

Competitors include Tesla, startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA, and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company.

Hyundai‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work.

Atlas and AI learn with human help

Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski. He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT, and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago.

In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts.

Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind. He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming.

This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously.

The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors.

Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints.

Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI ​​system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking.

Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas.

What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI ​​revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works.

One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it.

Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility

There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year.

The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics.

It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement.

Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.”

“Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world.

Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns?

It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots.

But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade.

The humanoid robot race continues

Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win.

Are they ahead of us?

The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind.

To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us.

Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

AI moves toward superhuman capabilities

When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind.

A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge.

“I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.”

“I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.”

Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills.

“So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.”

From AGI to robotics

As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in.

Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out.

Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware?

“I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.”

“If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.”

Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning.

“There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI ​​systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?”

Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.”

Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. It announced its Gemini 2 foundation model in August and Gemini 4 Argon this week.

Anduril founder says robots and AI can reduce risk

Some international groups call such weapons killer robots. But Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, said they represent the future of warfare—a working product that eliminates risks. Once a child prodigy, Luckey sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion.

He ultimately decided to move into the defense industry. The billionaire owns an autonomous speedboat called Dive XL. It is not remote-controlled, and Anduril claimed that it can travel 1,000 miles fully submerged. Australia has already invested $58 million in such submarines.

Tucked away inside a hangar is an Anduril unmanned fighter jet called the Fury. It has no cockpit, control stick, or rudder because there’s no pilot. Some in the defense industry viewed Anduril as just another tech startup until it beat out several leading defense contractors in the competition to build an unmanned fighter jet for the U.S. Air Force.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

]]> It should come as no surprise to hear that the UK is growing from strength to strength when it comes to startup investment, with new research revealing billions in funding for university spinouts, larger investment rounds in Cambridge and a wave of funding for DefenceTech.

But while investors appear increasingly willing to back established, capital-intensive businesses, the figures also reveal a growing challenge for startups seeking their first investment.

Three recently published studies from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), Parkwalk and Beauhurst, and White & Case offer a common thread connecting the British funding landscape in 2026.

The numbers are notable. UK university spinouts secured €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) in the first half of 2026, Greater Cambridge’s early-stage businesses have raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015, and 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and technology startups expect to seek significant external funding over the next 12 months.

So, is Britain Europe’s leading startup investment destination?

Universities and their billion-pound momentum

Greater Cambridge is one of the clearest examples of the UK’s growing capacity to attract investment into technology companies.

According to analysis published by Cambridge Innovation Capital for the Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026, early-stage businesses in the region have collectively raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015.

More significantly, the average equity raised per deal has increased fivefold over the decade, rising from €2.3 million (£2 million) in 2015 to €11 million (£10 million) in 2025. Greater Cambridge’s life sciences and DeepTech businesses also reportedly attracted more funding per deal on average in 2025 than their counterparts in London, Greater Oxford and Greater Manchester.

The findings suggest that Cambridge is developing beyond its traditional role as a university research hub into an ecosystem capable of producing companies that attract larger investment rounds.

Cambridge’s momentum is reflected in several startups previously covered by EU-Startups. Battery technology company Nyobolt raised €26.3 million in April 2025, before reaching a $1 billion valuation in 2026. Meanwhile, AI materials discovery startup CuspAI secured €393.2 million in July 2026 at a €2.2 billion valuation, while launching an AI Materials Foundry involving NVIDIA.

More recently, DefenceTech company Cambridge Aerospace raised €259.7 million in August 2026 at a €2.94 billion valuation.

Dr Michael Anstey, Partner at Cambridge Innovation Capital and board member Innovate Cambridge, said: “A fivefold increase in average deal size over ten years shows how far Cambridge’s innovation economy has matured. Investors are backing Cambridge companies with larger rounds because there is now a proven route from world-class research to businesses that can scale globally.” 

The growing size of Cambridge investment rounds reflects a wider pattern across UK university spinouts.

Research from Parkwalk and private company data provider Beauhurst found that UK university spinouts raised €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) across 215 deals in H1 2026, the second-highest half-year total recorded over the past decade and a 38.2% increase on H2 2025.

Much of this funding went into advanced technologies. Four companies alone – Quantum Motion, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Fractile and CellCentric – accounted for €846 million (£709 million), with Oxford Quantum Circuits securing the period’s largest round at €301 million (£260 million).

Defence funding takes off

Beyond university spinouts, another sector attracting investor attention is defence technology.

New research from White & Case reveals that 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and DefenceTech startups are likely to raise significant external funding over the next 12 months.

The study, conducted by Censuswide among 250 senior decision-makers in the UK defence and military sector between 17 and 24 September 2026, suggests that companies are preparing to scale in response to growing demand for advanced defence capabilities.

Businesses are considering a range of financing options, including equity investment, debt and government grants. Among surveyed companies, 49% intend to seek equity financing, 47% debt financing and 39% government grants.

Equity is particularly relevant to DefencetTech startups, with 59% considering this funding route, compared with 49% of established defence companies. Many younger businesses are still developing their products and have yet to generate significant revenues, making traditional debt financing more difficult.

Government-backed investors were identified as the most attractive equity funding source by 37% of businesses seeking equity, followed closely by corporate venture investors, strategic corporate investors and private equity firms.

Daniel Turgel, Partner and Co-head of White & Case’s Global Technology Industry Group, commented: “For the most promising businesses, there is no lack of equity financing. A wall of private capital is looking for a home in defence technology as previous investment restrictions are relaxed and investors rush to gain exposure to a highly attractive sector, with long-term structural growth tailwinds that extend beyond current conflicts and even defence itself.”

The findings suggest that DefenceTech could become another important contributor to UK startup investment, alongside established areas such as FinTech and life sciences.

Interest is being supported by rising military expenditure, government efforts to develop domestic technological capabilities and the potential dual-use applications of technologies initially developed for defence.

Big cheques, fewer first rounds

While the total value of investment into UK university spinouts is approaching record levels, the Parkwalk and Beauhurst findings reveal a more complicated picture for early-stage founders.

First-time equity investment fell from €176 million (£148 million) in H1 2025 to €56 million (£47 million) in H1 2026, a decline of 68.3%.

The number of first-time funding deals also decreased, from 47 to 44 over the same period, significantly below the peak of 73 recorded in H1 2021.

Meanwhile, later-stage investment reached €907 million (£760 million) in H1 2026, its highest half-year level since 2021, representing a 165% year-on-year increase.

The contrast is significant. Although more capital is flowing into established university spinouts, fewer emerging businesses are securing their first equity investment.

Moray Wright, CEO of Parkwalk, said: “British DeepTech is attracting capital at a scale we have rarely seen, and that is something to celebrate. But these figures carry a clear warning. First-time investment has fallen, and the companies vital to the future of the UK economy are struggling to raise their first round.”

The shift is also visible in average deal sizes, which have more than doubled over the past decade, from €4.2 million (£3.57 million) in H1 2016 to €8.6 million (£7.24 million) in H1 2026.

The growth of later-stage financing is a positive sign for the UK, but the shrinking pool of first-time funding raises questions about whether the country is building a sufficiently broad pipeline of new businesses to sustain its investment momentum.

Global money, British innovation

Another finding connecting the three studies is the UK’s growing relationship with international investors.

According to Parkwalk and Beauhurst, funding rounds involving at least one international investor accounted for 86.1% of total university spinout investment in H1 2026, the highest share recorded this decade.

British investors nevertheless remain central to the ecosystem. Since 2016, UK investors have participated in 2,545 spinout deals, more than six times the 408 involving US investors.

Yet international investment also introduces questions about where the value generated by British innovation ultimately ends up.

International buyers accounted for 75% of UK spinout acquisitions in H1 2026 and 68.3% of acquisitions since 2016. Over the decade, US buyers acquired 66 UK spinouts, compared with 57 acquired by British buyers.

The geographical distribution of funding presents another challenge. Nearly 80% of spinout investment since 2016 has gone to the South East, East of England and London.

University of Oxford spinouts have raised €6.4 billion (£5.39 billion) over this period, compared with €4.7 billion (£3.99 billion) for University of Cambridge spinouts. Further north, Manchester university spinouts attracted €232 million (£195 million), while those in Liverpool secured €23.3 million (£19.6 million).

So, on top of there being a clear difficulty in directing funding to early-stage companies, there seems to be a higher amount of foreign investment circulating than national funding across an imbalanced geography. Bringing into question the future interests of these companies, their investors and eventual market goals.

Conclusion

Wether the UK can translate their clear financial strength into long-term European leadership will depend on more than headline investment totals.

Ensuring early-stage founders can access funding, encouraging investment beyond established innovation hubs and helping British companies remain and grow in the country will be equally important.

The UK’s startup funding lead does not simply depend on how much capital it can attract, but how widely that capital can support the next generation of companies.

]]> Enact Intelligence, a physical AI startup headquartered in Zurich, has come out of stealth today with a €26.68 million ($30 million) pre-Seed funding round, one of the largest pre-Seed raises in Europe to date.

The round saw participation from institutional investors redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital, alongside a notable slate of angel investors, including Arthur Mensch, founder of Mistral; Yann LeCun, founder of AMI Labs and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta; and Andrew Lonsberry, founder of Path Robotics.

“Dexterity is the next frontier in robotics, and Enact is tackling it with a new data modality: starting with high precision force data from bespoke actuators they are rethinking the entire stack from the hardware up. We are very excited about Enact’s approach of leveraging orthogonal data to improve existing models and build a data moat,” said Dr. Harald Nieder, General Partner of redalpine.

Founded in March 2026 by Manuel Yves Galliker, Enact is building robots that can not only see their environment but physically sense what is happening when they interact with it. Before founding Enact, Galliker led the software team for the humanoid robot NEO at 1X, helped build 1X’s AI team in Silicon Valley, and went on to work at the robotics lab Physical Intelligence.

The central argument of Enact is that most robots today depend almost entirely on vision to perceive their surroundings, limiting their ability to manipulate objects reliably or learn efficiently from experience. Existing haptic sensing solutions, which extend robots with force and touch, are either too costly or fragile for meaningful industrial deployment.

To solve this physical AI challenge, Enact rethinks the entire stack, from model architectures and data pipelines through to the actuators and sensors that feed the model. As a departure from traditional robots relying on point-based force sensors, Enact’s robots capture force data directly from the actuators themselves, similar to how humans sense tension through their muscles rather than solely through their fingertips.

Manuel Yves Galliker, CEO and founder of Enact Intelligence, said, “Unlike the early days of LLMs, physical AI has the advantage of starting from strong reasoning, language, and vision capabilities already in place. Instead of trying to collect every piece of data needed to teach a robot common sense about the world, we can build on top of existing models, like video models, and adapt them to output robot actions for interacting with the real world. So what we are addressing is the ability to efficiently learn from experience and perform tasks reliably, both of which require the model to understand the physics of the robot and the task at hand.”

This approach, Galliker argues, will lead to the development of “a proprioceptive nerve system and the cortex that makes sense of it,” solving dexterity through whole-body force-awareness at a cost and reality-level suitable for industrial scale.

Enact’s twelve-person team draws its engineering talent from DeepMind, 1X, Amazon Robotics, Helsing, Physical Intelligence and ETH Zurich. Alongside the funding, the company announced bringing Philip Kneis, a former DeepTech investor at redalpine, to lead growth.

“Silicon Valley has traditionally been very strong in software and AI, but it’s lacking in robotics and hardware engineering talent, and with the current excitement around robotics a lot of money is chasing a few people. What we will do is bring the AI experience with us from Silicon Valley and combine it with Zürich’s local talent pool. That’s the winning formula,” added Galliker.

The fresh capital will be used to grow its team fivefold by the end of 2027, accelerate its hardware and R&D pipelines, and roll out its robots with multiple industrial partners across manufacturing, infrastructure, retail, and food processing.

]]> Photon Bridge (formerly Photon IP), an Eindhoven-based startup building optical engines for AI and telecom, has raised €10 million to tackle an emerging bottleneck in AI infrastructure: producing the millions of lasers needed to connect increasingly large clusters of AI processors.

New investors, the Amadeus APEX Technology Fund and 360 Capital, co-led the round, while existing investors Innovation Industries, Faber, and Brabant Development Agency (BOM) also increased their investment. In January 2025, the company announced it had secured a €4.75 million Seed round led by Innovation Industries. 

“Every new wave of compute creates new bottlenecks further down the supply chain, and lasers are the next one. Photon Bridge is addressing this with a technology that combines deep photonics expertise with a credible path towards manufacturing at very large scale,” said Ion Hauer, Investment Partner at APEX Ventures. 

Photon Bridge was founded in 2020 in Eindhoven by Rui Santos and Xaveer Leijtens to rethink how high-performance photonic systems are built at scale. The company says it is building laser sources for a market expected to need millions of units as optical connections move closer to AI chips.

It develops high-power, multi-wavelength laser-source technology for next-generation optical interconnects in AI data centres.

According to the startup, data transfer between processors is becoming a performance constraint as AI clusters expand from thousands to hundreds of thousands of chips. It notes that optical connections can move enormous amounts of data faster and more efficiently than conventional electrical interconnects, prompting their integration closer to processors. 

It also notes that this shift is accelerating with the emergence of co-packaged optics, which integrates optical connectivity directly alongside the chips that move data through AI systems. The startup says that this, in turn, drives demand for the lasers that supply light to these connections.

“Today’s high-power laser supply chain was largely built for telecom and subsea networks, where volumes are far lower. AI could transform the laser from a specialist photonics component into something that has to be manufactured at semiconductor scale. Photon Bridge has designed its technology around that transition,” the company mentioned in the press release 

Rather than generating the required optical power using a small number of increasingly powerful lasers, Photon Bridge claims that it combines and multiplexes light from multiple lower-power semiconductor lasers.

The Dutch startup says this approach reduces power densities, making individual lasers less sensitive to manufacturing defects, improving production yield and allowing Photon Bridge’s architecture to scale more efficiently as volumes increase.

The platform is designed to deliver high wavelength counts with up to 40 mW of optical power per wavelength per fibre, while enabling production across multiple indium phosphide (InP) foundries.

In September 2025, Photon IP rebranded as Photon Bridge and appointed Paul Marchal as CEO.

Marchal, CEO of Photon Bridge, said, “AI is fundamentally changing the way computing infrastructure is built. We are moving towards enormous systems in which hundreds of thousands of processors have to operate together, and moving data between them is becoming one of the defining constraints on performance.

“That means optics has to move closer to the compute. But it also creates an entirely different manufacturing challenge. The industry will soon need millions of these laser sources every year. Instead of making individual lasers increasingly powerful and difficult to manufacture, we move that scaling challenge into the architecture.”

Photon Bridge highlights that its approach is designed around manufacturing yield, a consideration that becomes increasingly important as laser production shifts from traditional telecom volumes to the scale required by AI infrastructure.

“AI is turning lasers from a telecom component into a semiconductor-scale product. Once you start talking about millions of units a year, manufacturing yield becomes fundamental. Photon Bridge has designed its architecture from the beginning around the volumes this market is going to require,” said Cesare Maifredi, Partner at 360 Capital.

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate product development and customer qualification, deliver its first samples in 2027, and prepare for volume manufacturing from 2028. Photon Bridge will also expand its Eindhoven team as it moves toward commercialisation.

The Axe is developed under the leadership of CTO Dr. William Brooks, who has spent over three decades in light aircraft development and has certified more than 2,000 aircraft currently in service. Axe takes off like a helicopter using eight fixed-angle electric motors, transitions to forward flight where its wings generate aerodynamic lift and can operate from conventional runways.

Since there are no tilting motors or rotary wings, Axe is designed to eliminate the mechanical complexity and potential points of failure that characterise many eVTOL concepts. In an emergency power loss scenario, the winged design allows the aircraft to glide rather than fall. 

The Axe offers a range of over 100 miles, a flight time of 60 to 90 minutes, a cruising speed of 100mph and a 200kg payload capacity. Skyfly projects an operating cost of around €83.57 (£70) per flight, which gives it a favourable standing against the likes of legacy two-seater aircrafts such as Robinson R22 or Cessna 152.

Longbow, Skyfly’s second aircraft, is a hybrid-electric unmanned aircraft with a range exceeding 400 miles and the same 200kg payload. It is designed for cargo resupply, intelligence and surveillance, medevac, and ship-to-shore logistics missions. The company says both the aircraft will be manufactured at Skyfly’s 10,000 sq.ft. facility in Thorpe Mandeville, Oxfordshire.

“Longbow addresses a clear requirement for unmanned systems that can move meaningful payloads over significant distances without relying on a runway. Archangel invests exclusively in defence-first companies, and our backing of Skyfly reflects the potential we see in its technology to deliver mission necessary capability for the modern battlespace,” said Nicholas Nelson, General Partner at Archangel Ventures.

Skyfly says its Axe prototype has completed more than 100 piloted flights, including Europe’s first airfield-to-airfield eVTOL flight. It holds experimental flight permits in both the UK and the US, and sixty-one private customers globally have already placed orders. 

The fundraise comes amid a regulatory shift, with the FAA’s MOSAIC reforms taking effect in July 2026. The MOSAIC reforms rewrote the rules governing Light Sport Aircraft to admit electric propulsion, multi-motor architectures and vertical take-off aircraft into a category that has been historically restricted to private owners rather than commercial operators. Skyfly says its Axe, a two-seat electric Vertically Capable Aircraft (eVCA) classified as Light Sport-class, was designed precisely for this rulebook.

Michael Thompson, founder and CEO of Skyfly, said, “This investment gives us the resources to take the Axe from a flying prototype to a certified aircraft in customers’ hands. The FAA’s MOSAIC rules have opened a route to market that simply did not exist for electric aircraft before, and the Axe was designed for exactly this category. HICO and Archangel understood that timing, and their backing lets us move at the pace the opportunity demands: completing certification and standing up series production.”

The fresh capital will be deployed across three areas: completing FAA Light Sport Aircraft certification for the Axe under the MOSAIC rules, scaling manufacturing capacity on both sides of the Atlantic, and accelerating development of the Longbow.

]]> sennder, a German digital road freight forwarder, today announced that it will hit €1 billion in annual revenue for this year, as well as completing the integration of C.H. Robinson’s European operations.

The delivery scale-up has raised over €340 million in funding and is now on track to deliver IFRS EBITDA profitability for the full year of 2026. sennder now operates as one business on one platform, sennOS, moving more than 150,000 shipments a month through a network of more than 40,000 vetted carriers.

“Continued operational momentum and sustained profitability puts us in an even stronger position to invest in the digital transformation of freight,” says David Nothacker, co-founder and CEO of sennder. “We brought two large businesses onto one platform and lifted operator productivity by 45% in the process, and this milestone reinforces sennder’s role as a dependable partner for customers and carriers alike and enables us to keep raising the standard for reliability, efficiency and innovation in European road freight.”

To understand sennder’s landmark, it is important to look at the wider transport/cargo sector in Europe and the developing competition – as well as the funding being distributed in 2026.

These include Berlin-based cargo.one with nearly €17 million for multimodal freight software and Ukraine-based Cargofy with €5.2 million in primary funding for AI-powered freight operations.

In Germany, FRYTE Mobility raised €3.5 million for electric truck charging coordination and NexDash secured €2.5 million for road-freight electrification, while Belgium’s Vectrix raised €1.15 million for transport-order automation.

These announcements represent approximately €29.4 million in new company funding.

EU-Startups previously covered sennder’s €131.2 million Series D in 2021 and CEO David Nothacker’s discussion of the C.H. Robinson transaction in 2025.

Founded in 2015, sennder is a digital road freight forwarder, leveraging data and technology to increase efficiency and transparency in road logistics, with the aim of reducing empty miles and optimising transport flows.

sennder connects shippers with a broad network of carriers, with the goal of enabling low-emission, cost-effective transport while supporting carriers in navigating a traditionally fragmented industry.

Over the past 12 months, these initiatives have prevented more than 31,000 tonnes of CO2e emissions.

For sennder, today’s achievement is driven by putting profitability and revenue quality ahead of volume growth, actively optimising its customer portfolio.

Operator productivity, measured as gross profit per operator, rose 45% YoY. sennder attributes the increase to scale, the single integrated platform and its growing use of reasoning AI agents which work alongside teams, supporting them in serving customers at scale.

The AI agents reason across vast volumes of live network data to match loads with the right capacity, price shipments in real time and resolve issues before they escalate, streamlining operations further.

With profitability established, sennder will continue to invest in its platform, its AI agents and its European carrier network. The focus is profitable growth: growing volume that is sustainable and supports reliable service for customers and carriers.

]]> YGO, a Berlin-based startup building an AI infrastructure layer for the travel industry, raised €8 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Ventech, with participation from Sake Bosch, Caesar and Business Angels. In August 2024, the company announced it had secured €2.5 million in funding led by GetAway Group. 

“Online travel booking is undergoing its biggest structural shift in decades but most of the industry’s infrastructure was never built for it. YGO’s customers are already re-owning their customer relationships with AI and putting real KPI uplifts on the board to prove it. That’s why we believe YGO’s neutral infrastructure will become critical to how travel operates in an AI-first world,” said Nicolas Barthalon, Partner at Ventech.

Founded in 2023 by Julian Kögel, Sebastian Kreutzberger, and Willi Ibbeken, YGO sits at the intersection of legacy travel technology and the emerging ecosystem of AI agents. The company’s platform connects travel companies, including tour operators, online travel agencies, and travel agencies, directly with airlines, hotels, and tour operator inventory, without the need to restructure their existing booking infrastructure.

YGO does this by structuring and enriching fragmented hotel and product data, giving it the depth and accuracy that AI agents need to reliably discover, compare and recommend travel products. Its content enrichment product automatically generates verified, structured hotel data and delivers it across a company’s own digital channels and to external AI assistants via MCP (Model Context Protocol).

Its Hotel Q&A product embeds an AI-powered question-and-answer layer directly onto hotel pages, allowing travellers to ask any question and receive verified answers in real time and in their own language. Its AI Distribution product, on the other hand, makes a travel company’s entire hotel portfolio accessible and bookable through AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

YGO says online travel agencies and metasearch platforms have captured 15-25% of every booking, acting as intermediaries between travellers and suppliers. With AI assistants becoming the starting point for travel planning and booking, suppliers are looking for ways to reclaim direct relationships with their customers.

The platform already processes bookings for major European travel players including Condor, Bentour, and GetAway Group. YGO says their collaboration has led to a 90% reduction in manual operations and a 20% improvement in conversion for one airline client, and a 2.4x increase in average order value with no additional headcount for another.

“Travel is one of the last major industries still built on infrastructure that was never designed for an AI-first world. We built YGO to change that: to give the travel industry the infrastructure to make its inventory accessible, bookable and ready for AI – whether through their own platforms or through external AI agents,” said Kögel, co-founder and CEO of YGO.

YGO has grown its recurring ARR into seven figures within six months and has processed more than €15 million in bookings through its infrastructure to date. The fresh capital will be utilised to scale go-to-market and sales operations, deepen its AI orchestration platform, and expand the company’s customer base beyond the DACH region, targeting both enterprise accounts and mid-sized travel companies.

“This funding allows us to build on the strong business we already have with some of Europe’s leading travel players and become the AI infrastructure layer connecting the industry to the next generation of travel,” added Kögel.

]]> EstateMin, an Irish-founded LegalTech startup helping trust and estate law firms manage estate values with its AI-powered platform, has secured €1 million in pre-Seed funding.

The funding round saw participation from NDRC, First Port Syndicate, and Enterprise Ireland, which invested through its High Potential Start-Up programme. Angel investors Mike Hanrahan, Moira McKenna, and Conor Stanley also participated alongside other Irish angels.

“The real benefit for our clients is how much easier EstateMin makes it to get us information. Executors and family members can complete their intake right from the portal, on their own time, instead of juggling calls and paperwork during an already difficult process. That means their matter moves faster and they spend less time chasing us for updates,” said James Greenwood of Greenwood Law in Illinois.

Founded in Ireland in 2024 and now headquartered in Brooklyn, New York, EstateMin was built to solve a problem its co-founder and CEO, Isabella Hughes, experienced firsthand. A law graduate and former international boxer, Hughes spent time working as a legal executive, manually retyping client information into legal documents, a time-consuming process that she describes as unnecessary.

To solve this problem, she teamed up with Oisín Dolphin, a machine learning expert with over eight years of experience, who was drawn to the same problem after going through probate following the death of his father. The two met at an NDRC founder weekend at Dogpatch Labs in 2024. John Noonan, who brings more than four years of experience across product and consumer success at legal technology company Clio, subsequently joined as the third co-founder.

“What Oisín was describing was something I was doing every day. You don’t necessarily question it when it’s simply part of your job. Then somebody points out that you’re taking information a client has already provided and typing it all over again, and suddenly you realise how much time is being lost,” said Hughes, co-founder and CEO of EstateMin.

EstateMin’s AI-powered platform helps attorneys manage estate planning, estate administration and trust matters by digitising client intake, organising estate information, extracting data from documents and supporting form preparation. Its AI Case Reviewer scans files to flag missing fields, inconsistencies, or additional forms needed before a submission is finalised.

The platform integrates with existing legal case management systems, including Clio, and the company says it can become operational in about two minutes with minimal configuration. The platform is already helping trust and estate law firms manage more than €686 million ($770 million) in estate values across 777 matters.

Law firms reportedly save five to seven hours on each estate planning matter and five to ten hours on estate administrations. The platform is active across all 50 US states, and EstateMin is reporting 20% month-on-month revenue growth.

The journey to this point hasn’t been easy, with Hughes recounting a pivotal moment where they had to decide between the US and the UK. After initially building for Irish law firms and seeing slower adoption than expected, Hughes said they didn’t have the money to try everywhere and choose between the UK or take the bigger risk and expand to America.

“The response we’d had in New York was completely different, so we decided to go for it,” she explained.

The pre-Seed funding is earmarked for customer acquisition in the US, scaling EstateMin’s go-to-market operations, and expanding its engineering and product teams. The company has already hired two software engineers and added US business development capacity as part of its US push.

“EstateMin started with a very simple problem: why are highly trained legal professionals spending so much time retyping information? We’ve gone from working on that problem in Dogpatch Labs to building specifically for firms across America. Now we want to see how far we can take it,” Hughes added.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }

 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;

 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}

 margin-bottom: 14px;

 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;

.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>
